# Netjes

> React apps and sites on ASP.NET Core. C# owns routing, loaders, server actions, authorization and caching; a supervised pool of Node sidecars renders React; the browser hydrates and navigates. Pages follow the Next.js App Router conventions in `app/`.

<!-- Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/README.md -->

![Netjes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/assets/netjes-lockup.svg#gh-light-mode-only)
![Netjes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/assets/netjes-lockup-on-ink.svg#gh-dark-mode-only)

# Netjes

[![CI](https://github.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/actions/workflows/ci.yml)

**Build React apps and sites on ASP.NET Core.** *Netjes* is Dutch for neat and tidy, said "NET-yes".

Netjes is a React framework for .NET teams. You write pages in `app/` with the Next.js App Router conventions, and the server side in C#: ASP.NET Core receives every request and owns routing, data loading, server actions, authorization and caching. A supervised pool of Node processes renders the React tree to HTML, the browser hydrates it, and later navigations fetch the next page's props as JSON from the same C# endpoints.

## Why Netjes

- **The server is ASP.NET Core.** Loaders and actions are minimal API handlers, with dependency injection, model binding, ASP.NET Core authentication and `RequireAuthorization()`, and the data access you already use. There is no second server to deploy or keep in step.
- **The pages are React.** Layouts, loading and error boundaries, client navigation, Suspense and streaming, with Vite, Tailwind CSS, TanStack Query and Vitest set up.
- **Types come from C#.** The C# records are the source: `generated/netjes.ts` holds zod schemas, typed server action references and typed routes, so a renamed property or a mistyped link is a type error.
- **Forms work without JavaScript.** A form that calls a C# server action posts as a plain HTML form when scripts are off, and comes back with its errors and what was typed.

## A small example

A page, its C# loader and a server action. `Program.cs` registers Netjes and maps the feature:

```csharp
builder.Services.AddNetjes();
builder.Services.AddSingleton<PostStore>();

var app = builder.Build();
app.UseNetjes();
app.UseAntiforgery(); // after authentication, if you have it

app.MapPostPages();
app.MapPages(); // every other page file, plus the 404 fallback
app.Run();
```

```csharp
// Features/Posts/PostPages.cs
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc; // for [FromForm]

public static class PostPages
{
    public sealed record PostProps(string Slug, string Title, string Body, int Likes);

    public sealed record LikeInput
    {
        public string Slug { get; init; } = "";
    }

    public static void MapPostPages(this IEndpointRouteBuilder app)
    {
        // The page's loader, in place of a server component: it binds like a minimal API handler.
        app.MapPageLoader("/blog/[slug]", (string slug, PostStore posts) =>
            posts.Find(slug) is { } post
                ? Page.Props(new PostProps(post.Slug, post.Title, post.Body, posts.LikesOf(slug)))
                    .WithMetadata(new PageMetadata { Title = post.Title })
                : Page.NotFound());

        // A server action: POST /_netjes/actions/posts.like, behind antiforgery and an origin check.
        app.MapAction("posts.like", ([FromForm] LikeInput input, PostStore posts) =>
        {
            if (posts.Find(input.Slug) is null)
            {
                return ServerAction.NotFound();
            }

            posts.Like(input.Slug);
            return ServerAction.Ok().Refresh(); // the page loads again, with the new count
        });
    }
}
```

```tsx
// app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx
import { Form, Link, definePage, useAction } from 'netjes';
import { pages, route, serverActions } from '../../../generated/netjes.ts';

// pages['/blog/[slug]'] is the zod schema of the C# PostProps record.
export default definePage(pages['/blog/[slug]'], function Post({ slug, title, body, likes }) {
  const [, like, pending] = useAction(serverActions['posts.like']);
  return (
    <article>
      <Link href={route('/blog')}>All posts</Link>
      <h1>{title}</h1>
      <p>{body}</p>
      {/* Without JavaScript this is a plain form post, and the page comes back with the new count. */}
      <Form action={like}>
        <input type="hidden" name="slug" value={slug} />
        <button disabled={pending}>Like ({likes})</button>
      </Form>
    </article>
  );
});
```

`app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx` is the route `/blog/{slug}`. ASP.NET Core matches it, runs the loader, and renders the page on the server; `<Link>` then navigates in the browser. The app rewrites `generated/netjes.ts` when it starts in development, so `pages['/blog/[slug]']` and `serverActions['posts.like']` follow the C# records.

## Quick start

You need the .NET 10 SDK and Node.js 22.22.2 or a later 22, 24.15.0 or a later 24, or 26 or newer (the odd releases 23 and 25 are not supported).

```bash
npx netjes new my-app
cd my-app
npm run dev          # http://localhost:5080
```

`netjes new` writes an ASP.NET Core app with a root layout, a page with a C# loader, a form calling a validated server action, component tests, Tailwind CSS, the generated types, and Docker files for development and production. Edit a page and the browser updates through Vite; edit the C# and `dotnet watch` applies it.

[Getting started](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/getting-started.md) takes that app from the first page to a deployed container. If you know the Next.js App Router, [Coming from Next.js](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/coming-from-nextjs.md) maps each of its concepts to the Netjes counterpart.

## Features

- **Routing** with the App Router file conventions: layouts, templates, `loading`, `error`, `not-found`, `forbidden` and `unauthorized` boundaries, route groups, dynamic, catch-all and optional catch-all segments, parallel and intercepting routes, a client router with prefetching and back and forward from memory, base paths and locale routing. [Routing](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/routing.md)
- **Data loading** in C#: page loaders, layout loaders that are skipped on navigations within their section, shared props for every page, public configuration read at runtime, and TanStack Query seeded from the loader so queries render on the server. [Data loading](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/data-loading.md)
- **Server actions and forms**: C# endpoints with typed references, DataAnnotations validation, `<Form>` with a fallback without JavaScript, antiforgery and same-origin checks, revalidation, uploads and downloads. [Actions and forms](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/actions-and-forms.md)
- **Rendering and streaming**: streamed documents, `Page.Defer` for slow values, `loading.tsx` and Suspense, complete documents for crawlers, `dynamic()` and `clientOnly()`, and in production a page the browser renders itself while no Node process is ready. [Rendering and streaming](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/rendering-and-streaming.md)
- **Caching**: output-cached pages with tag and path revalidation, from actions or from anywhere, draft mode that bypasses the cache. [Caching](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/caching.md)
- **Metadata**: titles with templates, descriptions, Open Graph, Twitter and robots tags from page files or from C#, a sitemap and `robots.txt` from the route table, and `<Script>`. [Metadata](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/metadata.md)
- **Images**: `<Image>` with an optimiser endpoint, configured widths and allow-listed remote hosts, and optional resizing and WebP with SkiaSharp. [Images](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/images.md)
- **Static export**: `netjes export` writes every page as a complete HTML file. [Static export](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/static-export.md)
- **Security defaults**: security headers on every document, an opt-in Content-Security-Policy with nonces or hashes, body limits for actions, safe redirects and a guarded image endpoint. [Security](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/security.md)
- **Testing**: Vitest set up by the Vite plugin, a harness that renders pages and components with a fake router and fake actions, and C# tests against the real app. [Testing](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/testing.md)
- **Deployment**: `dotnet publish` runs the client build and ships it with the app; Docker, health checks, OpenTelemetry traces and metrics, several instances behind a load balancer. [Deployment](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/deployment.md)
- **Coding agents**: new apps come with an `AGENTS.md` and a Netjes skill, and the docs are published as `llms.txt` and `llms-full.txt`. [Coding agents](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/coding-agents.md)

Two example apps show the pieces together. The [Blog](https://github.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/tree/main/examples/Blog) has a catch-all docs section, a guestbook that works without JavaScript, a JSON API used through TanStack Query, streaming, images and a static export. [TaskBoard](https://github.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/tree/main/examples/TaskBoard) is a multi-tenant project tracker with cookie authentication, Postgres through EF Core, protected sections, optimistic updates, Testcontainers tests and a production Docker Compose stack behind a TLS proxy.

## Packages

| Package | What it holds |
|---|---|
| [`netjes`](https://github.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/tree/main/packages/netjes) on npm | The Vite plugin, the client router and components, the sidecar that renders pages, the `netjes` command and the app template |
| [`Netjes`](https://github.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/tree/main/src/Netjes) on NuGet | The ASP.NET Core library: routing from `app/`, loaders, server actions, rendering, caching, the image endpoint, type generation |
| [`Netjes.Images.SkiaSharp`](https://github.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/tree/main/src/Netjes.Images.SkiaSharp) on NuGet | Optional image processing for `<Image>`: resizing and WebP |

The three are released together under one version. An app uses the same version of `netjes` and `Netjes`, which `netjes new` pins and `netjes info` checks.

## Requirements

- The .NET 10 SDK. Apps target `net10.0`.
- Node.js 22.22.2 or a later 22, 24.15.0 or a later 24, or 26 or newer (`^22.22.2 || ^24.15.0 || >=26.0.0`), at build time and next to the app in production: the server renders pages in Node processes it starts and supervises.
- React 19, Vite 7 or newer, and zod 4 for the generated schemas. `netjes new` installs them.
- Docker, only for the template's container setup.
- Linux, macOS or Windows. CI runs the .NET and JavaScript tests on all three (the ones that need Docker on Linux only), and the end-to-end suites and the package check on Linux.

## Status

Netjes is at 0.0.1, its first release. Until 1.0, a new version can change the API; the [changelog](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/CHANGELOG.md) says what changed and what to do about it.

Not there yet:

- Showing the target's `loading.tsx` at once on a client navigation. The router waits for the next page's payload, then shows it.
- Metadata files in `app/` (`icon.png`, `opengraph-image.tsx`, `manifest.json`) and generated Open Graph images.
- Client navigation in static exports: exported pages navigate with full page loads.
- Intercepting folders outside a `@slot`.

The [roadmap](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/roadmap.md) has what comes next.

Left out by design:

- React Server Components. C# loaders do their job: data comes from C# as props, and every component ships to the browser ([ADR 0010](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/decisions/0010-app-router-with-csharp-layout-loaders.md)).
- Serverless and edge hosts. Pages render in long-lived Node processes next to the .NET app ([ADR 0001](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/decisions/0001-react-renders-in-node-sidecars.md)).

## Community

Questions and ideas go to [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/discussions), bugs to the [issue tracker](https://github.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/issues). Read [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) before a pull request, and follow the [Code of Conduct](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md). Report security problems privately, as [SECURITY.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/SECURITY.md) describes, not in the issue tracker.

# Getting started

This tutorial takes you from an empty folder to a Netjes app running in a container. You build a small notes app: a page, a C# loader that feeds it, a page per note, a server action with validation, a component test, a production build and a Docker image. It assumes you know some React and some C#; it explains the Netjes parts as they come up.

## Before you start

You need:

- the .NET 10 SDK or newer (`dotnet --version` shows 10 or higher);
- Node.js `^22.22.2 || ^24.15.0 || >=26.0.0`, that is Node.js 22.22.2 or a later 22, 24.15.0 or a later 24, or 26 or newer (`node --version`): the tools in the app, Vitest and jsdom among them, need these releases, and the odd releases 23 and 25 are not supported;
- Docker, for the last step only.

Netjes is tested in CI on Linux, macOS and Windows: the .NET and JavaScript tests on all three (the ones that need Docker on Linux only), and the end-to-end suites and the package check on Linux.

## Create the app

```bash
npx netjes new my-app
```

`netjes new` copies the app template into `my-app`, runs `npm install` in it, and prints where things are:

```text
Created MyApp in my-app (using the Netjes 0.0.1 packages)

  app/                 the pages: page.tsx is /, about/page.tsx is /about, layout.tsx wraps them
  components/          React components, each with a Vitest test
  Features/            the C# side, one folder per feature: loaders and server actions
  Program.cs           the ASP.NET Core app (MyApp.csproj)
  generated/netjes.ts  types and zod schemas from C#, rewritten by netjes generate; never edit it
  Dockerfile           and the docker-compose files: Docker for development and production

Next:
  cd my-app
  npm run dev    then open http://localhost:5080
```

The folder name gives the .NET project name and root namespace (`my-app` becomes `MyApp`); `--name Shop` picks another. The app references the `Netjes` NuGet package and the `netjes` npm package at the exact version that created it, since the two halves speak one protocol. [The netjes command](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/reference/cli.md#netjes-new) lists the options.

## What is in it

```text
my-app/
  app/
    layout.tsx               the root layout: the header, the navigation, the title template and the favicon
    page.tsx                 /, with props from a C# loader
    about/page.tsx           /about, a page without a loader
    not-found.tsx            unknown URLs, and Page.NotFound() from a loader
    error.tsx                errors below the root layout
  components/                Greeting.tsx and HelloForm.tsx, each with a *.test.tsx next to it
  Features/Home/HomePage.cs  the home page's loader and the home.greet server action
  Program.cs                 services and the request pipeline
  SiteProps.cs               the shared props every page and layout gets
  generated/netjes.ts        zod schemas, typed actions and routes, generated from the C# types
  styles/global.css          Tailwind CSS, imported by app/layout.tsx
  public/favicon.svg         the favicon, the Netjes mark until you put your own there
  MyApp.csproj, package.json, vite.config.ts, tsconfig.json
  appsettings.json, appsettings.Development.json
  Properties/launchSettings.json   the launch profile for dotnet run and IDEs
  Dockerfile, docker-compose.yml, docker-compose.override.yml, docker-compose.prod.yml
  AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, .claude/skills/netjes/   guides for coding agents
```

`Program.cs` is short. Every request goes through ASP.NET Core:

```csharp
using MyApp;
using MyApp.Features.Home;

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

builder.Services.AddNetjes(options =>
    // Available in every page and layout through useSharedProps(sharedProps); typed in generated/netjes.ts.
    options.UseSharedProps(_ => ValueTask.FromResult(new SiteProps("My App"))));
builder.Services.AddHealthChecks().AddNetjes();

var app = builder.Build();

if (!app.Environment.IsDevelopment())
{
    app.UseHsts();
    app.UseHttpsRedirection();
}

app.UseNetjes();
app.UseAntiforgery(); // after authentication, if you add it

app.MapHealthChecks("/healthz");
app.MapHomePage();
app.MapPages(); // every other page file, plus the 404 fallback

app.Run();
```

`UseNetjes()` serves static files, routes requests to pages and renders errors. Each feature maps its loaders and actions (`MapHomePage()`), and `MapPages()` comes last: it maps every page file that has no loader of its own, and the not-found page for everything else.

## Run the dev server

```bash
cd my-app
npm run dev
```

`npm run dev` runs `netjes dev`, which starts `dotnet watch` in the Development environment. The app starts a Node process that runs the Vite dev server, and renders pages through it. Open http://localhost:5080.

Two edits to try:

- In `components/Greeting.tsx`, change the button's text. The browser updates in place, keeping the click count: Vite's hot module replacement.
- In `Features/Home/HomePage.cs`, change `"Hello from C#"`. `dotnet watch` applies the change to the running app; reload the page to see it.

Hot reload applies changes inside methods. Code that runs once at startup, such as `Program.cs` and the `Map...` calls, needs a restart: press Ctrl+R in the terminal that runs `npm run dev`. Ctrl+C stops it. The app listens on another port with `ASPNETCORE_URLS=http://localhost:3000 npm run dev`. The Vite dev server has a port of its own, 5173: when another app's Vite dev server has it, `npm run dev` says so, and `Netjes__ViteDevPort=5174 npm run dev` moves it.

When the Vite dev server cannot start, the app says why in one log entry and stops, and `dotnet watch` waits: an error in `vite.config.ts` comes with Vite's code frame, and a package it imports that is not installed with the advice to run `npm install`. Fix it, then press Ctrl+R.

In Development, `appsettings.Development.json` limits `AllowedHosts` to `localhost`, `127.0.0.1` and `[::1]`: a request for any other host name gets a 400, so a hostile web page cannot point its own domain at your machine and read the dev app (DNS rebinding). Add a name there if you reach the dev server by another one.

### Debugging

To step through the C# code, start the app from your IDE, such as Visual Studio or Rider: it runs the launch profile in `Properties/launchSettings.json`, as `dotnet run` does, which starts the app in Development on http://localhost:5080 with its Node process and the Vite dev server, but without `dotnet watch`. Stop `npm run dev` first, since both use the same ports.

To keep `npm run dev` running, attach the debugger to the app's own process instead. `dotnet watch` builds the app and starts it as the executable named after the project: `MyApp`, or `MyApp.exe` on Windows. That process runs your C# code; the `dotnet` processes above it belong to `dotnet watch`, and the `node` process below it renders the pages. While a debugger is attached, .NET does not apply hot reload updates to that process, so C# edits reach it only when you restart with Ctrl+R; edits to the pages still update the browser as usual. Each restart (Ctrl+R, or an edit hot reload cannot apply) starts a new process, which you attach to again. The pages' own code runs in the browser too, where the browser's developer tools debug it.

## Add a page

Pages are React components in `app/`, named after the Next.js App Router conventions: `app/notes/page.tsx` is `/notes`. Create it:

```tsx
// app/notes/page.tsx
import type { Metadata } from 'netjes';

export const metadata: Metadata = { title: 'Notes' };

export default function Notes() {
  return (
    <section className="space-y-6">
      <h1 className="text-3xl font-bold tracking-tight">Notes</h1>
      <p className="text-slate-600">Nothing here yet.</p>
    </section>
  );
}
```

Open http://localhost:5080/notes. ASP.NET Core routes a new page file at once; the tab title is "Notes · My App", from the title template in `app/layout.tsx`. A page without a C# loader renders with empty props.

Links between pages are typed: `<Link href>` accepts the URLs of the app's pages, listed in `generated/netjes.ts`. The dev server rewrites that file when it starts; while it runs, update it yourself after adding a page:

```bash
npx netjes generate
```

Then add the page to the navigation in `app/layout.tsx`, next to the other two links:

```tsx
<Link href="/notes" className={navLink}>
  Notes
</Link>
```

`<Link>` navigates in the browser: it fetches the next page's props from the server as JSON, swaps the page in and keeps the layout mounted. [Routing](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/routing.md) covers the other file conventions: layouts, loading and error boundaries, route groups, catch-all segments, parallel and intercepting routes.

## Load data in C#

The page's data comes from a C# loader. Notes need somewhere to live; for this tutorial, memory will do. Create `Features/Notes/NoteStore.cs`:

```csharp
namespace MyApp.Features.Notes;

public sealed record Note(int Id, string Text, DateTimeOffset CreatedAt);

/// <summary>Notes kept in memory, until the app stops. A real app would use a database here.</summary>
public sealed class NoteStore(TimeProvider time)
{
    private readonly Lock _lock = new();
    private readonly List<Note> _notes = [];

    public IReadOnlyList<Note> All()
    {
        lock (_lock)
        {
            return [.. _notes.OrderByDescending(note => note.Id)];
        }
    }

    public Note? Find(int id)
    {
        lock (_lock)
        {
            return _notes.Find(note => note.Id == id);
        }
    }

    public Note Add(string text)
    {
        lock (_lock)
        {
            var note = new Note(_notes.Count + 1, text, time.GetUtcNow());
            _notes.Add(note);
            return note;
        }
    }
}
```

Then the loader, in `Features/Notes/NotesPages.cs`:

```csharp
namespace MyApp.Features.Notes;

public static class NotesPages
{
    public sealed record NotesProps(IReadOnlyList<Note> Notes);

    public static void MapNotesPages(this IEndpointRouteBuilder app)
    {
        app.MapPageLoader("/notes", (NoteStore notes) => Page.Props(new NotesProps(notes.All())));
    }
}
```

`MapPageLoader` maps the page at `/notes` with this delegate as its loader. It is a minimal API handler: its parameters bind from route values, the query string and services, and it can carry `.RequireAuthorization()` or any other endpoint convention. `Page.Props(...)` returns a `PageResult<NotesProps>`, which names the props type for the generated schema.

Register the store and map the feature in `Program.cs`:

```csharp
using MyApp;
using MyApp.Features.Home;
using MyApp.Features.Notes;

// ...
builder.Services.AddHealthChecks().AddNetjes();
builder.Services.AddSingleton<NoteStore>();

// ...
app.MapHomePage();
app.MapNotesPages();
app.MapPages(); // every other page file, plus the 404 fallback
```

That is startup code, so press Ctrl+R to restart. On start, the app rewrites `generated/netjes.ts` with schemas for the new records:

```ts
export const Note = z.object({
  id: z.number().int(),
  text: z.string(),
  createdAt: z.iso.datetime({ offset: true, local: true }),
});
export type Note = z.infer<typeof Note>;
export const NotesProps = z.object({
  notes: z.array(Note),
});
export type NotesProps = z.infer<typeof NotesProps>;

export const pages = {
  "/": HomeProps,
  "/about": z.object({}),
  "/notes": NotesProps,
} as const;
```

The schemas follow the JSON the app sends: camelCase names, `DateTimeOffset` as an ISO date string, nullability as declared. Now make the page read its props:

```tsx
// app/notes/page.tsx
import { Link, type Metadata, definePage } from 'netjes';
import { pages, route } from '../../generated/netjes.ts';

export const metadata: Metadata = { title: 'Notes' };

export default definePage(pages['/notes'], function Notes({ notes }) {
  return (
    <section className="space-y-6">
      <h1 className="text-3xl font-bold tracking-tight">Notes</h1>
      {notes.length === 0 ? (
        <p className="text-slate-600">Nothing here yet.</p>
      ) : (
        <ul className="space-y-2">
          {notes.map((note) => (
            <li key={note.id}>
              <Link href={route('/notes/[id]', { id: String(note.id) })} className="underline">
                {note.text}
              </Link>
            </li>
          ))}
        </ul>
      )}
    </section>
  );
});
```

`definePage` parses the props with the schema before the component sees them, and types them: `notes` is a `Note[]`. The `route('/notes/[id]', ...)` call is for the next step; it is a type error until that page exists.

If you change a C# type that reaches the browser while the dev server runs, hot reload applies the change, and the generated file stays as it was until the next start. Run `npx netjes generate`, or restart. [Data loading](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/data-loading.md) covers layout loaders, shared props, public configuration and seeding TanStack Query from a loader.

## A page per note

Square brackets make a dynamic segment. Add a loader for `/notes/[id]` to `MapNotesPages`, and a props record next to `NotesProps`:

```csharp
public sealed record NoteProps(Note Note);

// in MapNotesPages:
app.MapPageLoader("/notes/[id]", (int id, NoteStore notes) =>
    notes.Find(id) is { } note
        ? Page.Props(new NoteProps(note)).WithMetadata(new PageMetadata { Title = $"Note {note.Id}" })
        : Page.NotFound());
```

The `id` parameter binds the `[id]` route value by name, as in any minimal API. `Page.NotFound()` renders `app/not-found.tsx` with status 404, and `.WithMetadata(...)` sets the page's title from C#, which the layout's template completes. A value that is not a number, such as `/notes/abc`, does not bind, so it gets a 400 and the error page.

Create `app/notes/[id]/page.tsx`:

```tsx
import { Link, definePage } from 'netjes';
import { pages, route } from '../../../generated/netjes.ts';

export default definePage(pages['/notes/[id]'], function NotePage({ note }) {
  return (
    <article className="space-y-4">
      <Link href={route('/notes')} className="underline">
        All notes
      </Link>
      <p className="text-xl">{note.text}</p>
      <p className="text-slate-500">
        Written <time dateTime={note.createdAt}>{note.createdAt}</time>
      </p>
    </article>
  );
});
```

Restart with Ctrl+R, since `MapNotesPages` runs at startup. `route('/notes/[id]', { id })` builds the URL with the value encoded, and a missing or misspelt parameter is a type error.

## A server action with validation

Notes are added by a server action: a C# endpoint that React calls like a function, and that a plain form posts to when JavaScript is off. Add the input record and the action to `NotesPages.cs`:

```csharp
using System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc;

namespace MyApp.Features.Notes;

public static class NotesPages
{
    public sealed record NotesProps(IReadOnlyList<Note> Notes);

    public sealed record NoteProps(Note Note);

    public sealed record NewNote
    {
        [Required(ErrorMessage = "Write something first."), StringLength(200, ErrorMessage = "Keep it under 200 characters.")]
        public string? Text { get; init; }
    }

    public static void MapNotesPages(this IEndpointRouteBuilder app)
    {
        app.MapPageLoader("/notes", (NoteStore notes) => Page.Props(new NotesProps(notes.All())));

        app.MapPageLoader("/notes/[id]", (int id, NoteStore notes) =>
            notes.Find(id) is { } note
                ? Page.Props(new NoteProps(note)).WithMetadata(new PageMetadata { Title = $"Note {note.Id}" })
                : Page.NotFound());

        // Called from components/NewNoteForm.tsx as serverActions['notes.add'].
        app.MapAction("notes.add", ([FromForm] NewNote input, NoteStore notes) =>
        {
            notes.Add(input.Text!.Trim());
            return ServerAction.Ok().Refresh();
        });
    }
}
```

`MapAction("notes.add", ...)` maps `POST /_netjes/actions/notes.add`. It requires an antiforgery token, which `<Form>` adds, and a request from the app's own origin. Before the delegate runs, Netjes checks the DataAnnotations on its input; when they fail, the action answers 422 with the errors per field, and the delegate never runs. The input has `init` properties rather than constructor parameters, so a field the post leaves out, such as an unchecked checkbox, keeps its default instead of making form binding refuse the post ([Validation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/actions-and-forms.md#validation)). `.Refresh()` tells the browser to load the page on screen again, so the new note shows up.

The form, in `components/NewNoteForm.tsx`:

```tsx
import { Form, useAction } from 'netjes';
import { serverActions } from '../generated/netjes.ts';

export function NewNoteForm() {
  const [state, formAction, pending] = useAction(serverActions['notes.add']);
  const error = state?.ok === false ? state.errors.text?.[0] : undefined;
  return (
    <Form action={formAction} className="space-y-2">
      <label className="block space-y-1">
        <span className="font-medium">New note</span>
        <input
          name="text"
          defaultValue={state?.ok === false ? String(state.values?.text ?? '') : ''}
          aria-invalid={error ? true : undefined}
          aria-describedby={error ? 'text-error' : undefined}
          className="block w-full rounded-lg border border-slate-300 px-3 py-2 aria-invalid:border-red-600"
        />
      </label>
      {error && (
        <p id="text-error" className="text-sm text-red-700">
          {error}
        </p>
      )}
      <button type="submit" disabled={pending} className="rounded-full bg-slate-900 px-4 py-2 font-medium text-white">
        {pending ? 'Saving…' : 'Add note'}
      </button>
    </Form>
  );
}
```

Put `<NewNoteForm />` on the notes page, under the heading, with `import { NewNoteForm } from '../../components/NewNoteForm.tsx';`. Restart (the action is mapped at startup), and the generated file gains a typed reference:

```ts
export const serverActions = {
  "home.greet": serverAction<FormData, Greeting>("home.greet", { result: Greeting }),
  "notes.add": serverAction<FormData, void>("notes.add"),
} as const;
```

`useAction` wraps React's `useActionState`: `state` is `null` before the first post, `{ ok: true, result }` after a success, and `{ ok: false, errors, values }` after a failure. React resets a form after its action runs, so `values` hands back what was typed, for the `defaultValue`. The error keys are the JSON names of the input's properties (`text`).

Now turn JavaScript off in your browser's developer tools and add a note again. `<Form>` renders a real `<form method="post">` with the antiforgery token in a hidden field. A valid post redirects back to `/notes` (303); an invalid one renders the page again in the same request, with status 422, the error under the field and the text still in it. [Actions and forms](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/actions-and-forms.md) has the rest: JSON actions, page actions, redirects, revalidation, uploads, and what a failed post hands back.

## Test it

The template sets up Vitest with jsdom and Testing Library, and `netjes/testing` renders components inside a fake app: a router that records navigations, and server actions answered by your test. Create `components/NewNoteForm.test.tsx`:

```tsx
import { render, screen } from '@testing-library/react';
import userEvent from '@testing-library/user-event';
import { createTestApp } from 'netjes/testing';
import { expect, it } from 'vitest';
import { NewNoteForm } from './NewNoteForm.tsx';

it('shows the error from C# next to the field, and keeps what was typed', async () => {
  const app = createTestApp({
    actions: {
      'notes.add': () => ({ ok: false, status: 422, errors: { text: ['Keep it under 200 characters.'] } }),
    },
  });
  render(<NewNoteForm />, { wrapper: app.Wrapper });

  await userEvent.type(screen.getByLabelText('New note'), 'Far too long');
  await userEvent.click(screen.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add note' }));

  expect(await screen.findByText('Keep it under 200 characters.')).toBeDefined();
  expect(screen.getByLabelText<HTMLInputElement>('New note').value).toBe('Far too long');
});
```

Run the checks the template's `AGENTS.md` lists before you call a change done:

```bash
npm test                      # Vitest
npm run typecheck             # strict TypeScript, against the generated types
dotnet build                  # C#, with warnings as errors
npx netjes generate --check   # fails when generated/netjes.ts is out of date
npm run routes                # the route table, and warnings about likely mistakes
```

`netjes generate --check` belongs in CI: it runs the app once without serving anything or starting Node, and fails when the committed file no longer matches the C# types. [Testing](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/testing.md) covers page tests, C# tests of loaders and actions against the real app, and Playwright.

## Build and run in production

```bash
npx netjes build     # generated/netjes.ts, then dist/client and dist/server
npx netjes start     # the app in Production, on http://localhost:5000
```

`netjes build` regenerates the types and runs `vite build` and `vite build --ssr`: `dist/client/` holds the browser bundles, and `dist/server/` the server bundle and the script of the Node process that renders it. `netjes start` runs `dotnet run -c Release` in the Production environment. In production the app starts its Node process with the built bundle; there is no Vite dev server. The notes are in memory, so they are gone after a restart.

To deploy, publish the app:

```bash
dotnet publish -c Release -o bin/publish
cd bin/publish && dotnet MyApp.dll
```

The build leaves `bin/`, `obj/` and a `publish/` folder in the project out of the app's content, so publishing into any of them is safe.

`dotnet publish` runs `npm run build` and copies `dist/` into the output, through the build targets the `Netjes` package adds. It does not regenerate `generated/netjes.ts`, which is why CI runs `netjes generate --check`. The machine that runs the app needs Node.js as well as the ASP.NET Core runtime.

Outside Development the template sends HSTS on https responses, and redirects http to https once the app knows its https port (`ASPNETCORE_HTTPS_PORT`); until then it logs that it cannot determine the port. Behind a proxy that terminates TLS, add `UseForwardedHeaders()`, trusting only that proxy, before `UseNetjes()`.

## Run it in Docker

The template's `Dockerfile` has a development target and a production target, and three Compose files use them:

```bash
docker compose up                                                     # development: dotnet watch and Vite, http://localhost:8080
docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.prod.yml up -d # production, on port 8080
```

Development bind-mounts the source, so edits reload as they do outside Docker, and binds ports 8080 and 5173 to localhost only. The production image builds the client in one stage and publishes the app in another, then runs on the ASP.NET Core runtime image with a Node binary next to it, as a non-root user. The production Compose file makes the filesystem read-only, drops capabilities, limits CPU and memory, restarts the container, checks `/healthz`, and keeps ASP.NET Core's Data Protection keys, which sign antiforgery tokens, in a named volume. ASP.NET Core logs a warning that those keys are not encrypted at rest; configure one of its `ProtectKeysWith...` options to encrypt them.

The image restores `Netjes` from NuGet and `netjes` from npm, so it needs the `package-lock.json` that `npm install` wrote. [Deployment](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/deployment.md) covers configuration, health checks, telemetry, proxies and running several instances.

## Add Netjes to an existing app

To add Netjes to an ASP.NET Core project you already have:

1. Reference the NuGet package: `dotnet add package Netjes --version 0.0.1`. The package adds build targets to the project: `using Netjes` when `ImplicitUsings` is on, `node_modules` and `dist` kept out of the build, and `dotnet publish` running `npm run build` and shipping `dist/`.
2. Next to the project file, add a `package.json` with `"type": "module"` and the scripts `"dev": "netjes dev"`, `"build": "vite build && vite build --ssr"`, `"test": "vitest run"`, `"typecheck": "tsc -p tsconfig.json --noEmit"`, `"generate": "netjes generate"` and `"routes": "netjes routes"`. Install the npm half at the same version as the NuGet package (`netjes@0.0.1` with `Netjes` 0.0.1), and the tools the template builds, tests and type-checks with:

   ```bash
   npm install netjes@0.0.1 react react-dom zod @tanstack/react-query
   npm install -D vite typescript @types/react @types/react-dom tailwindcss @tailwindcss/vite \
     vitest jsdom @testing-library/react @testing-library/dom @testing-library/user-event
   ```
3. Add a `vite.config.ts`:

   ```ts
   import netjes from 'netjes/vite';
   import { defineConfig } from 'vite';

   export default defineConfig({ plugins: [netjes()] });
   ```
4. Add a `tsconfig.json`, the one `netjes new` writes. It type-checks `app`, `components`, `generated` and `vite.config.ts`:

   ```json
   {
     "compilerOptions": {
       "target": "ES2022",
       "module": "ESNext",
       "moduleResolution": "bundler",
       "lib": ["ES2023", "DOM", "DOM.Iterable"],
       "types": ["vite/client"],
       "jsx": "react-jsx",
       "strict": true,
       "noUncheckedIndexedAccess": true,
       "noImplicitOverride": true,
       "isolatedModules": true,
       "verbatimModuleSyntax": true,
       "allowImportingTsExtensions": true,
       "skipLibCheck": true,
       "noEmit": true
     },
     "include": ["app", "components", "generated", "vite.config.ts"]
   }
   ```

   `netjes` ships JavaScript with declaration files, so your `tsc` checks your own code alone, also under stricter options you add, such as `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` or `noPropertyAccessFromIndexSignature` (see [TypeScript setup](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/reference/vite-plugin.md#typescript-setup)).
5. Put pages in `app/`, with an `app/layout.tsx` that imports a stylesheet containing `@import "tailwindcss";`.
6. In `Program.cs`, call `builder.Services.AddNetjes()`, then `app.UseNetjes()`, `app.UseAntiforgery()` (after authentication) and `app.MapPages()`.
7. Run `npx netjes generate`, which writes `generated/netjes.ts` from the C# types; the app rewrites it each time it starts in Development. Commit it.
8. Start the dev server with `npm run dev` (the `netjes dev` script from step 2), or `npx netjes dev`. It runs the app with `dotnet watch` and Vite hot reloading, on `http://localhost:5080` unless `ASPNETCORE_URLS` says otherwise.

`npx netjes info` checks the result: Node.js and the SDK, the installed packages and their versions, the Vite config and the `app/` folder. [Vite plugin](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/reference/vite-plugin.md) lists the plugin's options, including how to turn Tailwind CSS, the query client or the Vitest defaults off.

## Next

- [Coming from Next.js](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/coming-from-nextjs.md), if you know the App Router.
- The [guides](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/README.md#guides), one per topic.
- The [Blog](https://github.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/tree/main/examples/Blog) and [TaskBoard](https://github.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/tree/main/examples/TaskBoard) examples, for a docs section, a guestbook, authentication, Postgres and streaming in working apps.

<!-- Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/coming-from-nextjs.md -->

# Coming from Next.js

This page is for developers who know the Next.js App Router. It maps each Next.js concept to its Netjes counterpart, then explains where the two differ. Netjes follows the App Router's file conventions in `app/` and its React APIs where it can, and does the server's part in ASP.NET Core and C#.

## Concept by concept

### Files and folders

| Next.js | Netjes |
|---|---|
| `app/` with `page.tsx` | The same. Page and segment files are `.tsx` or `.jsx`; every other file in `app/` is colocated code. [Routing](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/routing.md) |
| `layout.tsx` | The same, and it stays mounted across navigations. A root layout renders its content, not `<html>` and `<body>`: Netjes renders the document around it ([ADR 0003](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/decisions/0003-react-renders-the-whole-document.md)) |
| `template.tsx`, `loading.tsx`, `error.tsx`, `not-found.tsx`, `forbidden.tsx`, `unauthorized.tsx`, `global-error.tsx` | The same files. Built-in pages stand in for a missing `not-found.tsx` or `error.tsx`. `global-error.tsx` belongs at the root of `app/`; anywhere else it stops the app at startup |
| `[slug]`, `[...slug]`, `[[...slug]]`, `(group)`, `_private` | The same. Each page becomes an ASP.NET Core route (`[slug]` is `{slug}`), so ASP.NET Core's matcher decides precedence |
| Parallel routes: `@slot` folders, `default.tsx` | The same: the layout gets each slot as a prop |
| Intercepting routes: `(.)`, `(..)`, `(...)` | The same, inside a `@slot` folder. Intercepting folders outside a slot are not supported |
| `route.ts` | A minimal API endpoint (`app.MapGet`, `app.MapPost`). A `route.ts` file in `app/` stops the app in development and fails the production build, saying so |
| `middleware.ts` | ASP.NET Core middleware, in `Program.cs` |
| `public/` | `public/` |
| `sitemap.ts`, `robots.ts` | `app.MapSitemap(siteUrl)` and `app.MapRobotsTxt(siteUrl)`, built from the route table. [Metadata](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/metadata.md) |
| `icon.png`, `opengraph-image.tsx`, `manifest.json` | Not yet: set icons and Open Graph images through the Metadata API |
| `instrumentation.ts` | OpenTelemetry in `Program.cs`, with the `Netjes` ActivitySource and Meter. [Deployment](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/deployment.md) |

### Data

| Next.js | Netjes |
|---|---|
| A server component that fetches its data | A C# page loader: `app.MapPageLoader("/blog/[slug]", (string slug, PostStore posts) => Page.Props(...))`. It binds like a minimal API handler. [Data loading](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/data-loading.md) |
| A layout that fetches its data | A C# layout loader: `app.MapLayoutLoader("/dashboard", ...)`. It is skipped on navigations within its section while its route values and user stay the same |
| `getServerSideProps` (Pages Router) | `MapPageLoader` |
| `params` and `searchParams` | Loader parameters in C#; `useParams()` and `useSearchParams()` in React, each with an optional schema |
| `cookies()`, `headers()` | `HttpContext` or `HttpRequest` as a loader parameter, with the values passed on as props |
| `React.cache`, request memoization | Scoped services: one instance per request |
| Streaming a promise to a client component | `Page.Defer(task)` in the loader, read with `use()` inside a Suspense boundary, typed with `deferred(schema)`. [Rendering and streaming](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/rendering-and-streaming.md) |
| TanStack Query with `HydrationBoundary` | Built in: `.WithQuery(key, data)` on the loader's result seeds the query, so `useQuery` renders it on the server |
| `generateStaticParams` | `.StaticParams(...)` on the loader, for `netjes export` |
| `NEXT_PUBLIC_` environment variables | The `Netjes:PublicConfig` configuration section, read with `usePublicConfig(schema)` at runtime ([ADR 0009](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/decisions/0009-public-config-at-runtime.md)) |
| `draftMode()` | `IDraftMode` in loaders, `useDraftMode()` in React |

### Server actions and forms

| Next.js | Netjes |
|---|---|
| `'use server'` functions | `app.MapAction("posts.like", delegate)`, a C# endpoint at `/_netjes/actions/posts.like`, called from React through the generated `serverActions['posts.like']` ([ADR 0011](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/decisions/0011-server-actions-as-csharp-endpoints.md)). [Actions and forms](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/actions-and-forms.md) |
| `useActionState` | `useAction(action)`, which wraps it: `[state, formAction, isPending]` |
| `useFormStatus`, `useOptimistic` | React's own; they work inside `<Form action={formAction}>` |
| `<form action={fn}>` | `<Form action={formAction}>`, which also posts without JavaScript |
| Validating input with zod in the action | DataAnnotations or `IValidatableObject` on the action's input, checked before it runs; `ServerAction.Invalid(field, message)` for other errors |
| `redirect()` in an action | `ServerAction.Redirect(url)` |
| `revalidatePath`, `revalidateTag` | `ServerAction.Ok().RevalidatePath(path)` and `.Revalidate(tags)`; `IPageCache` outside actions |
| `refresh()` | `ServerAction.Ok().Refresh()`, or `useRouter().refresh()` |
| `serverActions.bodySizeLimit`, `serverActions.allowedOrigins` | `Netjes:ActionBodySizeLimit` (1 MB by default) and `Netjes:AllowedActionOrigins`, which admits same-site origins only: a cross-site post is refused even when its origin is listed. [Options](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/reference/options.md) |
| A form posting to an API route | `app.MapPageAction("/guestbook", delegate)` with `<Form method="post">`: the page's own POST handler, which renders the page again |

### Navigation

| Next.js | Netjes |
|---|---|
| `next/link` | `<Link>`: client navigation, prefetching on hover and focus, `aria-current` on the current page. [React API](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/reference/react-api.md) |
| `useRouter()` from `next/navigation` | `useRouter()`: `push`, `replace`, `prefetch`, `refresh`, `back`, `forward` |
| `usePathname`, `useSearchParams`, `useParams`, `useSelectedLayoutSegment(s)` | The same names, from `netjes` |
| `notFound()`, `forbidden()`, `unauthorized()` | `Page.NotFound()`, `Page.Forbidden()`, `Page.Unauthorized()`, returned from a page or layout loader |
| `redirect()`, `permanentRedirect()` | `Page.Redirect(url)` and `Page.Redirect(url, permanent: true)`; `Page.LocalRedirect(url)` for a URL taken from the request |
| The client router cache | The router shows the last 50 pages again on back and forward without a request, and forgets them when an action signs someone in or out ([ADR 0014](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/decisions/0014-signing-in-or-out-clears-what-back-shows.md)) |
| `basePath` | `app.UsePathBase("/docs")` and `netjes({ basePath: '/docs' })` |
| i18n routing | A `[lang]` folder with `AddNetjesLocalization`, `UseNetjesLocalization` and `MapLocaleRedirect`; `useLocale()` in React |
| `redirects`, `rewrites`, `headers` in `next.config.js` | ASP.NET Core's URL Rewriting middleware, YARP and middleware. [Redirects, rewrites and headers](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/redirects-rewrites-headers.md) |

### Metadata, images and scripts

| Next.js | Netjes |
|---|---|
| `export const metadata` | The same, on pages and layouts: title templates, description, Open Graph, Twitter, robots, canonical. Twitter tags that are not set fill in from Open Graph and the page's title and description, as in Next.js |
| `generateMetadata` | `.WithMetadata(new PageMetadata { Title = post.Title })` on the loader's result, merged over the files' metadata |
| `next/head` | `metadata`, or React 19's own `<title>` and `<meta>` |
| `next/script` | `<Script strategy="afterInteractive">`, `lazyOnload` or `beforeInteractive` |
| `next/image` | `<Image>` and the `/_netjes/image` endpoint: configured widths, allow-listed remote hosts, WebP with `Netjes.Images.SkiaSharp`. [Images](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/images.md) |
| `images.remotePatterns`, `deviceSizes`, `imageSizes` | `Netjes:Images:RemoteHosts` and `Netjes:Images:Widths` |
| `next/dynamic` | `dynamic(() => import('./Chart.tsx'), { ssr: false })`, and `clientOnly(Component)` |
| `next/font` | Not built in: load fonts with CSS, as in any Vite app |

### Caching

| Next.js | Netjes |
|---|---|
| Static by default | Dynamic by default: every page renders per request, and goes out `no-store`, since pages carry per-user shared props and antiforgery tokens. [Caching](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/caching.md) |
| ISR, `export const revalidate` | `.CachePage(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30))` on the loader, on ASP.NET Core output caching |
| `export const dynamic` and other segment config | Endpoint conventions on the loader: `.CachePage(...)`, `.StaticParams(...)`, `.RequireAuthorization()` |
| On-demand revalidation in a route handler | `IPageCache.RevalidatePathAsync(path)` and `RevalidateTagAsync(tag)`, from any endpoint or background job |
| `unstable_cache`, the fetch cache | .NET's own caching (`IMemoryCache`, `HybridCache`) in your services |

### Tooling

| Next.js | Netjes |
|---|---|
| `create-next-app` | `npx netjes new my-app`. [Getting started](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/getting-started.md) |
| `next dev`, `next build`, `next start` | `netjes dev`, `netjes build`, `netjes start`; `dotnet publish` runs the build and ships it. [The netjes command](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/reference/cli.md) |
| `output: 'export'` | `netjes export`. Exported pages navigate with full page loads. [Static export](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/static-export.md) |
| `next.config.js` | `NetjesOptions` in C# (and the `Netjes` configuration section) for the server, `netjes()` options in `vite.config.ts` for the build. [Options](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/reference/options.md), [Vite plugin](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/reference/vite-plugin.md) |
| Typed routes | Generated from the page files: `route('/blog/[slug]', { slug })`, and `<Link href>` checks its URL |
| Fast Refresh, Turbopack | Vite with React Fast Refresh ([ADR 0004](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/decisions/0004-vite-for-dev-server-and-builds.md)) |
| Tailwind CSS setup | On by default in `netjes()`: `@import "tailwindcss"` in a stylesheet the root layout imports |
| Jest or Vitest, `next-router-mock` | Vitest defaults in `netjes()`, and `createTestApp()` from `netjes/testing`. [Testing](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/testing.md) |
| `useReportWebVitals` | `useReportWebVitals` from `netjes/vitals`; `<WebVitals />` sends them to .NET metrics |
| CSP nonces through middleware | `NetjesOptions.ContentSecurityPolicy` with `{nonce}`, and `useNonce()`. [Security](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/security.md) |

## The real differences

### No React Server Components

In Next.js a server component can query a database and render without shipping its code. Netjes has no server components: data comes from C# loaders as JSON props, and every component is a client component that renders on the server and hydrates in the browser ([ADR 0010](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/decisions/0010-app-router-with-csharp-layout-loaders.md)). So:

- Data access, secrets and authorization live in C#, never in a component. A component cannot reach anything the loader did not send.
- `'use client'` and `'use server'` mean nothing to Netjes; a `'use client'` line left in a component has no effect.
- Every component's code reaches the browser. Keep heavy, server-only work in C#, and load large client-only parts with `dynamic()`.
- A slow value does not hold the page up: return it with `Page.Defer(task)` and the document streams, with `loading.tsx` or a `<Suspense>` fallback until it arrives.

### Server actions are C# endpoints

A server action is a named minimal API endpoint, not a function whose identity the bundler encodes. Its name, such as `notes.add`, is stable across builds and deploys, and everything ASP.NET Core does for an endpoint applies to it: authorization, rate limiting, filters, logging. Every action requires an antiforgery token and a same-origin request, and Netjes checks the DataAnnotations of its input before it runs. The React side calls it through a reference generated from the C# signature, and a `<Form>` that uses it posts as a plain HTML form when JavaScript is off.

### Typed contracts generated from C#

There is no shared TypeScript between server and client to keep in step by hand. `generated/netjes.ts` is written from the C# types, through the same System.Text.Json contracts the app serializes with: zod schemas for page and layout props, shared props and JSON endpoints, typed server action references, and the app's routes ([ADR 0006](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/decisions/0006-types-and-zod-from-csharp-contracts.md)). `definePage` parses the props with the schema, so a payload that does not match fails with an `Invalid props` error before the component renders. The app rewrites the file in development; you commit it, and `netjes generate --check` fails CI when it is stale.

### ASP.NET Core owns the request

Routing is ASP.NET Core endpoint routing, built from the files in `app/` ([ADR 0002](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/decisions/0002-server-owns-routing.md)). The client router never matches URLs itself: it asks the server for every page. That puts the rest of the request in ASP.NET Core too:

- Authentication is ASP.NET Core authentication. `.RequireAuthorization()` on a page loader, a layout loader or `MapPages()` protects pages, and a failed check renders `unauthorized.tsx` or `forbidden.tsx`.
- A layout loader is skipped on navigations within its section, like Next.js's partial rendering, so it sees only the route values of its own URL. An access check on a deeper route value, such as a project id below `/projects`, belongs in the page's loader.
- Middleware, rate limiting, output caching, CORS, health checks and OpenTelemetry are the ASP.NET Core features you already know.
- Configuration is .NET configuration: `appsettings.json`, environment variables, secrets stores. Public values reach the browser at runtime, so one build runs in every environment.

### Rendering runs in Node, next to .NET

The server renders React in a pool of Node processes that the .NET app starts, health-checks and restarts ([ADR 0001](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/decisions/0001-react-renders-in-node-sidecars.md)). You deploy one ASP.NET Core app with Node.js installed next to it, in a container or on a server. There is no edge or serverless target. In production, while no Node process is ready, documents go out for the browser to render, so pages keep working through a restart ([ADR 0013](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/decisions/0013-client-rendered-fallback.md)).

### Pages are dynamic until you cache them

Next.js prerenders what it can. Netjes renders every page per request and sends it `no-store`, because pages carry the visitor's shared props and an antiforgery token. Caching is opt-in per page with `.CachePage(...)`, and a cached page must not depend on who is asking ([ADR 0016](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/decisions/0016-page-cache-rules-under-any-output-caching.md)).

### Smaller differences

- On a client navigation the router waits for the next page's payload, then shows it; it does not show the target's `loading.tsx` first. `loading.tsx` shows while a document or a navigation streams deferred values.
- `openGraph`, `twitter`, `alternates` and `icons` in `metadata` merge key by key down the layouts, the page and the C# metadata, where Next.js replaces each of these objects whole at every level that sets it. A page's `openGraph: { title }` keeps a layout's `siteName` and images, and a layout's `twitter.images` still make the card `summary_large_image` on a page that sets `twitter: { title }`. A page replaces a layout's key by setting it, `images: []` for none ([Metadata](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/metadata.md#titles-and-tags-from-page-files)).
- `notFound()`, `redirect()` and the like are not thrown from React components: the loader decides, in C#, before anything renders.
- There is no Pages Router. An app with Pages Router files in `pages/` stops at startup and says what to do with each: a page moves to its `app/` name (a `.js` page to a `.jsx` file), `404.tsx` to `app/not-found.tsx`, `500.tsx` and `_error.tsx` to `app/error.tsx`, `_app.tsx` and `_document.tsx` to the root layout, and an API route in `pages/api/` becomes a minimal API endpoint ([Routing](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/routing.md#what-is-not-there)).

## Moving an app over

1. Create an app with `npx netjes new` and move the components across; the `app/` file names are the same.
2. Rewrite each server component's data fetching, `getServerSideProps` or `generateMetadata` as a C# loader, returning a record of props.
3. Turn `'use server'` functions into `MapAction` endpoints, and route handlers into minimal APIs.
4. Move `middleware.ts` and the `next.config.js` redirects, rewrites and headers into `Program.cs`.
5. Replace `NEXT_PUBLIC_` variables with `Netjes:PublicConfig`.
6. Run `npm run routes`: it prints the route table as ASP.NET Core sees it, with warnings for loader parameters that miss a route value, for pages that match the same URLs, and for form inputs that refuse a post without a checkbox.

<!-- Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/routing.md -->

# Routing

This guide is for app developers. It covers how the files in `app/` become URLs, how pages link to each other and navigate in the browser, and how a component reads the URL. The conventions are the Next.js App Router's; [Coming from Next.js](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/coming-from-nextjs.md) lists where Netjes differs. Data for pages and layouts comes from C# loaders, described in [Data loading](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/data-loading.md).

## Pages

A page is a `page.tsx` file whose default export is a React component. Its folder path under `app/` is its URL:

```text
app/
  layout.tsx                  wraps every page
  page.tsx                    /
  about/page.tsx              /about
  blog/page.tsx               /blog
  blog/[slug]/page.tsx        /blog/hello-world
  docs/[...path]/page.tsx     /docs/getting-started/routing
```

```tsx
// app/about/page.tsx
import type { Metadata } from 'netjes';

export const metadata: Metadata = { title: 'About' };

export default function About() {
  return <h1>About</h1>;
}
```

A page without a C# loader renders with no props. A page with one reads its props through `definePage` and the generated schema ([Data loading](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/data-loading.md#reading-props-in-a-page)).

Page files are `.tsx` or `.jsx`. Tests next to them (`page.test.tsx`, `page.spec.jsx`) are not pages, and any other file in a folder is an ordinary module you can import.

Each page file becomes an ASP.NET Core endpoint with a route template: `blog/[slug]` is `/blog/{slug}`, `docs/[...path]` is `/docs/{**path:minlength(1)}` and `shop/[[...filters]]` is `/shop/{**filters}`. `app.MapPages()` maps every page that has no loader of its own, plus a fallback that renders the 404 page; `app.MapPageLoader(pattern, ...)` maps a page with a loader. Because they are endpoints, the ASP.NET Core matcher decides precedence, and conventions such as `.RequireAuthorization()` work as they do on any minimal API. The browser never matches routes itself: it asks the server for every page ([ADR 0002](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/decisions/0002-server-owns-routing.md)).

## Layouts, boundaries and other special files

A folder can hold these files next to its `page.tsx`:

| File | What it does |
|---|---|
| `layout.tsx` | Wraps every page in and below the folder. It stays mounted while the user navigates between those pages, so its state survives. |
| `template.tsx` | Like a layout, but mounted again on every navigation to another path. |
| `loading.tsx` | The Suspense fallback while a page below waits for deferred values or code. |
| `error.tsx` | The error boundary for the pages below the folder's layout. |
| `not-found.tsx` | Rendered when the loader of a page in or below the folder returns `Page.NotFound()`. The root one also renders for unknown URLs. |
| `forbidden.tsx` | Rendered for `Page.Forbidden()` and for an empty 403 from authorization. |
| `unauthorized.tsx` | Rendered for `Page.Unauthorized()` and for an empty 401 from authorization. |
| `global-error.tsx` | In `app/` only: rendered without any layout when even the error page fails. |
| `default.tsx` | In a `@slot` folder only: what a [parallel route](#parallel-routes) renders when no page in it matches. |

Per folder they nest as the App Router nests them: layout, then template, then error boundary, then the `loading.tsx` Suspense boundary, then the folder below or the page.

### Layouts

A layout gets `children` and the page's `params` (`LayoutProps`). The root layout, `app/layout.tsx`, wraps every page; it is where the global stylesheet is imported and the site's title template is set:

```tsx
// app/layout.tsx
import { Link, type LayoutProps, type Metadata, useSharedProps } from 'netjes';
import { sharedProps } from '../generated/netjes.ts';
import '../styles/global.css';

export const metadata: Metadata = { title: { default: 'My App', template: '%s · My App' } };

export default function RootLayout({ children }: LayoutProps) {
  const site = useSharedProps(sharedProps);
  return (
    <div>
      <header>
        <Link href="/">{site.siteName}</Link>
      </header>
      <main>{children}</main>
    </div>
  );
}
```

React renders the whole document ([ADR 0003](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/decisions/0003-react-renders-the-whole-document.md)): Netjes writes `<html>`, `<head>` and `<body>` around the root layout, so a layout returns what goes inside the body. Tags such as `<title>` and `<link rel="icon">` that a layout or page renders end up in the head.

A layout that needs data gets it from a C# layout loader, `app.MapLayoutLoader(...)`, and declares it with `defineLayout` ([Layout loaders](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/data-loading.md#layout-loaders)). A layout loader's conventions, such as `.RequireAuthorization()`, cover every page below it.

### Error, not-found, forbidden and unauthorized pages

An `error.tsx` gets `{ error, reset }` (`ErrorPageProps`). `error.status` holds the HTTP status when the server rendered the page for an error, and `reset()` renders the segment again:

```tsx
// app/error.tsx
import type { ErrorPageProps } from 'netjes';

export default function ErrorPage({ error, reset }: ErrorPageProps) {
  return (
    <section role="alert">
      <h1>Something went wrong</h1>
      {/* In development the message can take several lines: a syntax error comes with a code frame. */}
      <p style={{ whiteSpace: 'pre-wrap' }}>{error.message}</p>
      <button type="button" onClick={reset}>Try again</button>
    </section>
  );
}
```

An error boundary sits inside its folder's layout, so it catches errors in the pages and folders below, not in that layout itself. To catch an error in a layout, put an `error.tsx` in the folder above. On the server, an exception in a loader or a render gets the nearest `error.tsx` above the failing segment, with status 500 (or the status of a `BadHttpRequestException`).

`Page.NotFound()`, `Page.Forbidden()` and `Page.Unauthorized()` from a page loader render the nearest `not-found.tsx`, `forbidden.tsx` or `unauthorized.tsx`, in the page's folder or one above it, inside the layouts above that file, with status 404, 403 or 401. Without a `forbidden.tsx` or `unauthorized.tsx` the error page renders instead. Authorization that answers an empty 401 or 403 gets the same pages; with cookie authentication, answer those statuses instead of redirecting to a login page, as the TaskBoard example does:

```csharp
options.Events.OnRedirectToLogin = context =>
{
    context.Response.StatusCode = StatusCodes.Status401Unauthorized;
    return Task.CompletedTask;
};
```

Netjes has built-in 404 and error pages for apps that have neither file. Special pages can export `metadata` like any page, and the layouts' title templates apply to them ([Metadata](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/metadata.md)).

## Dynamic segments

| Folder | Matches | `params` in React | What a loader binds |
|---|---|---|---|
| `[slug]` | one segment: `/blog/hello` | `{ slug: 'hello' }` | `string slug` = `"hello"` |
| `[...path]` | one or more segments: `/docs/a/b` | `{ path: ['a', 'b'] }` | `string path` = `"a/b"` |
| `[[...path]]` | none or more: `/docs`, `/docs/a/b` | `{ path: [] }`, `{ path: ['a', 'b'] }` | `string? path` = `null`, `"a/b"` |

A catch-all must be the last segment. Parameter names are letters, digits and underscores, not starting with a digit, and each name appears once in a route, in any case. Literal segments match in any case, as ASP.NET Core routes do, but route values reach loaders and `params` as the URL spelled them.

Build URLs with `route()` from the generated file, which encodes each value and takes catch-all values as arrays:

```tsx
import { route } from '../generated/netjes.ts';

route('/blog/[slug]', { slug: post.slug });          // '/blog/hello-world'
route('/docs/[...path]', { path: ['guides', 'a b'] }); // '/docs/guides/a%20b'
route('/projects/[id]', { id }, { done: 2 });          // '/projects/web?done=2'
```

## Route groups and private folders

A folder in parentheses, `(marketing)`, adds nothing to the URL. Use it to give some pages a layout of their own: `app/(marketing)/layout.tsx` and `app/(app)/layout.tsx` can both sit at `/`, each wrapping its own pages. If two groups put layouts at one URL, a layout loader names the folder rather than the URL: `app.MapLayoutLoader("app/(app)", ...)`.

A folder whose name starts with `_`, such as `_components`, is not routed, so components can live next to the pages that use them.

## Parallel routes

A folder named `@slot` is a slot of the layout in the folder above it. The layout gets each slot as a prop named after the folder, without the `@`:

```text
app/dashboard/
  layout.tsx              gets { children, team, activity }
  page.tsx                /dashboard
  settings/page.tsx       /dashboard/settings
  @team/page.tsx          the team slot at /dashboard
  @team/default.tsx       the team slot at /dashboard/settings
  @activity/page.tsx      the activity slot at /dashboard; at /dashboard/settings it renders nothing
```

```tsx
// app/dashboard/layout.tsx
import type { LayoutProps } from 'netjes';
import type { ReactNode } from 'react';

export default function DashboardLayout({ children, team, activity }: LayoutProps & { team: ReactNode; activity: ReactNode }) {
  return (
    <div className="grid grid-cols-3">
      <main className="col-span-2">{children}</main>
      <aside>{team}{activity}</aside>
    </div>
  );
}
```

On every request and every client navigation, the server picks what each slot renders: the slot's page whose path below the layout matches the current page (parameters match by position, `[...x]` covers any depth, and the most specific page wins), else the slot's `default.tsx`, else nothing (the prop is `null`). A slot page gets its own route values as `params`, under its own parameter names. Inside a slot folder only `page` and `default` files count.

## Intercepting routes

An intercepting route shows another page inside a slot, the way a photo opens in a modal over a feed. It is a folder inside a slot whose name starts with `(.)` (the slot's own level), `(..)` (one level up; `(..)(..)` two), or `(...)` (the root), followed by the path it intercepts:

```text
app/
  layout.tsx                        renders the modal slot next to children
  feed/page.tsx                     /feed
  photo/[id]/page.tsx               /photo/7: the full page
  @modal/default.tsx                renders nothing
  @modal/(.)photo/[id]/page.tsx     /photo/7 in the modal slot
```

A client navigation to `/photo/7` from a page inside the slot's layout keeps that page on screen, with its state, and renders the intercepting page in the slot. The intercepting page gets the props of the real page's loader and its own `params`. Back closes it, and `router.refresh()` keeps it open over the page it opened on. A document request, such as a reload or a shared link, always shows the real page. Intercepting folders work only inside a slot.

## Linking and navigating

### Links

[`<Link>`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/reference/react-api.md#link) renders an `<a>` and navigates in the browser: it asks the server for the next page's props as JSON, loads the page's code, and swaps it in while the layouts above stay mounted.

```tsx
import { Link } from 'netjes';
import { route } from '../generated/netjes.ts';

<Link href={route('/blog/[slug]', { slug: post.slug })}>{post.title}</Link>
<Link href="/about" className="aria-[current=page]:font-bold">About</Link>
```

- `href` is typed by the app's routes once `netjes generate` has written `generated/netjes.ts`: a path no page serves is a type error. `Href.parse(value)` from the generated file checks a URL that comes from data, such as a CMS ([Typed links](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/data-loading.md#typed-links)).
- The link gets `aria-current="page"` when its path is the current one, for styling the current link.
- It prefetches the next page on hover, focus and touch. `prefetch="none"` turns that off. A prefetched page is kept for 30 seconds, and every server action or form post drops the ones kept so far.
- After navigating, the page scrolls to the top, or to the element the `#fragment` names. `scroll={false}` keeps the scroll position, and `replace` replaces the history entry instead of adding one.
- Ctrl-, Cmd-, Shift- and Alt-clicks, other mouse buttons, a `target` other than `_self`, a `download` attribute and URLs on another origin are left to the browser, as for a plain `<a>`. `reloadDocument` makes the browser load the URL with a full page load, for a file download or a page outside Netjes.

### Back and forward

The router remembers the last 50 pages it showed, one per history entry, and shows them again on back and forward without asking the server, restoring the scroll position. An action or form post that sets or deletes a cookie, such as signing in or out, makes it forget them, so those pages are loaded from the server again ([Signing in and out](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/actions-and-forms.md#signing-in-and-out)).

A fragment link to the same page (`#comments`) changes the history entry and scrolls, without a request. When it adds an entry, Back scrolls to where the page was, also for a link followed while the page was still hydrating.

### `useRouter`

```tsx
import { useRouter } from 'netjes';

const router = useRouter();
await router.push('/projects');               // navigate, adding a history entry
await router.replace(route('/login', {}, { returnUrl }), { scroll: false });
router.prefetch('/projects/web');             // load ahead, as a link does on hover
await router.refresh();                       // run this page's loaders again
router.back();
router.forward();
```

`refresh()` loads the page on screen from the server in place: every loader runs again, layout loaders included, in the same history entry, with the URL's fragment, without scrolling. `push`, `replace` and `refresh` return promises that settle when the navigation has finished.

### Navigation state

`useNavigation()` reports what the router is doing, for a progress bar or a disabled button:

```tsx
import { useNavigation } from 'netjes';

export function ProgressBar() {
  const navigation = useNavigation();
  return <div aria-hidden="true" data-state={navigation.state} className="progress" />;
}
```

`state` is `'idle'`, `'loading'` (a navigation) or `'submitting'` (a form post), and while it is not idle, `location` is the path and query on their way. After a form post that did not produce a page (an error response, or no response at all), `state` is `'idle'` with `error: { status, action }` until the next navigation; `status` is `null` when nothing answered.

### When the router hands over to the browser

The router falls back to a full page load when a navigation fails, when the server's answer is not a Netjes page, and when the page comes from another build of the app (after a deploy) or names a page this build does not have. A redirect to another site, from a loader or an action, is a full page load too. The router only ever loads pages from the document's own origin, and never navigates to a URL that is not http or https.

A navigation also fails when a module of the next page does not load: the request for its chunk was dropped, or a deploy removed the chunk. The browser then loads that page in full. On the first page of a document, a module that fails to load is tried once more, half a second later. If it fails again, the page stays as the server rendered it, without the client router, and the browser console names the module. Its links and forms work as plain HTML, so the next page the visitor opens is a full page load, and that document starts the router again. The [client-rendered fallback](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/rendering-and-streaming.md#when-no-sidecar-is-ready) has no page HTML to fall back on, so it stays blank.

### Forms that navigate

A `<Form method="get">` builds a query string from its fields and navigates to it, so filters live in the URL, work without JavaScript and can be shared. TaskBoard's board filters its tasks this way:

```tsx
<Form method="get" aria-label="Filter tasks">
  <input name="q" type="search" defaultValue={search.q ?? ''} />
  <button type="submit">Apply</button>
</Form>
```

Forms that post are covered in [Actions and forms](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/actions-and-forms.md).

## Reading the URL

| Hook | Returns |
|---|---|
| `usePathname()` | The path, without the base path: `/blog/hello`. |
| `useSearchParams()` | The query string as `URLSearchParams`. |
| `useSearchParams(schema)` | The query string parsed by a schema. |
| `useParams()` | The route values: `{ slug: 'hello' }`, catch-all values as arrays. |
| `useParams(schema)` | The route values parsed by a schema. |
| `useSelectedLayoutSegment()` | In a layout: the segment one level below it, or `null` at the layout's own page. |
| `useSelectedLayoutSegments()` | In a layout: all the segments below it. |

The [React API](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/reference/react-api.md#navigation) has their signatures. Visitors type URLs, so parse what you read with a schema. `useSearchParams(schema)` gets each value as a string, or an array of strings when a key repeats, and drops the values the schema rejects so its defaults and optional fields apply, rather than failing the page. `useParams(schema)` throws to the error page when a value is rejected, so constrain route values in C# (a loader returning `Page.NotFound()`) instead. Define schemas at module level: a new schema object on every render parses again.

```tsx
import { definePage, useParams, useSearchParams } from 'netjes';
import { z } from 'zod';
import { TaskPriority, pages } from '../../../../generated/netjes.ts';

// ?priority=whatever is dropped, so the filter falls back to "any".
const filters = z.object({
  q: z.string().optional(),
  priority: TaskPriority.optional(),
  done: z.coerce.number().int().positive().optional(),
});
const params = z.object({ id: z.string() });

export default definePage(pages['/projects/[id]'], function Board({ columns }) {
  const { id } = useParams(params);
  const search = useSearchParams(filters);
  // ...
});
```

`useSelectedLayoutSegment(s)` count from the layout's own folder, leave route groups out (they are not in the URL) and decode each segment. A layout uses them for tabs:

```tsx
// In app/projects/[id]/layout.tsx: 'settings' at /projects/web/settings, null at /projects/web.
const tab = useSelectedLayoutSegment();
```

## Base path

To serve the app under a path, such as `/docs`, set the base path on both sides:

```csharp
app.UsePathBase("/docs"); // before UseNetjes()
app.UseNetjes();
```

```ts
// vite.config.ts
export default defineConfig({ plugins: [netjes({ basePath: '/docs' })] });
```

Write links, form actions, redirects and router calls as if the app were at the root (`route()` builds paths that way): `<Link>`, `<Form>`, `useRouter()`, `Page.Redirect` and `ServerAction.Redirect` add the base path, except to paths that already start with it. `usePathname()` and `useNavigation()` locations leave it out.
