The endpoint for the page file runs its C# loaders (the layouts' and the page's), and Netjes builds the page payload: which page and layouts to show, their props, the route parameters, the shared props and the seeded queries. The next step depends on who asked:

- A document request (a browser loading the URL) sends the payload to a Node process, the sidecar, which renders the whole HTML document with React and streams it back. The payload is embedded in the document, and the browser hydrates it.
- A client navigation (`<Link>`, `router.push`, a `<Form>` post) asks the same URL for the payload as JSON. No Node process is involved: the browser loads the page module and renders it itself.

Only document requests need the sidecar. Redirects, not-found and forbidden results, authorization and the response status are all decided in .NET before anything is rendered.

## The sidecar pool

Netjes starts the Node processes when the app starts and stops them when it stops. You do not run or deploy them yourself: `UseNetjes()` and `AddNetjes()` are enough, as long as `node` is on the path (`NetjesOptions.NodeExecutable` names another one).

- In development there is one process. It also runs the Vite dev server (port 5173, `ViteDevPort`), which compiles your pages on demand, so an edit shows on the next request.
- In production each process imports the server build in `dist/server/`. `NetjesOptions.SidecarProcesses` sets how many run (default 1). A process renders one page at a time on one core, so an app whose pages take real CPU time to render wants about one per core. Each render goes to the ready process with the fewest renders in flight.

```json
{
  "Netjes": {
    "SidecarProcesses": 4
  }
}
```

The app does not start until every process has reported ready, within `StartupTimeout` (60 seconds). When a process cannot be started at all (Node.js is not found, or the sidecar script is not installed or built), or in development the Vite dev server does not start, the app logs why in one log entry, with what to do, and exits with code 1. A process listens on a random port on `127.0.0.1`, accepts only requests that carry the token .NET gave it, and exits when the app's end of its standard input closes, so it never outlives the app.

### Timeouts

| Option | Default | Limits |
|---|---|---|
| `RenderTimeout` | 15 s | How long a process may take to render the shell of a streamed document: everything outside Suspense boundaries that are still waiting. |
| `StreamTimeout` | 60 s | How long a whole document may take, deferred values and Suspense boundaries included. A complete document (for a crawler, below) waits up to this long. |

A render that runs out of time fails with the error page.

### Restarts

A process that exits is restarted after 1 second, then after 2, 4, 8 and 16 seconds for each crash in a row, and after 30 seconds from then on. The delay goes back to 1 second once a process has stayed up for 30 seconds. Each exit is logged with the last lines the process printed.

Renders while a process is down go like this:

- A render that has already been sent to the process when it dies fails with the error page. Netjes never sends it again, because it may be the render that brought the process down.
- A render that finds its process gone before anything was sent goes to another ready process, or, when there is none, waits for the restart within its own `RenderTimeout` (`StreamTimeout` for a complete document). A render with deferred values stays on the process it started on and waits for that one.
- In production, a document request that finds no process ready at all does not wait: it gets the [client-rendered fallback](#when-no-sidecar-is-ready).

Waiting for a restart applies with `ClientRenderFallback` off, in development, to `netjes export`, and to the render that is first to find its process gone. Other production documents get the fallback.

### Health

`AddNetjes()` on the health checks builder adds a check named `netjes`:

```csharp
builder.Services.AddHealthChecks().AddNetjes();
// ...
app.MapHealthChecks("/healthz");
```

It reports Healthy when every process is ready, Degraded while some are restarting (renders go to the others), and Unhealthy when none is ready. The template's Docker health check calls `/healthz`. See [deployment](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/deployment.md#health-checks).

## Streamed documents

A document streams. The sidecar sends the shell as soon as it is ready, with a fallback in place of each Suspense boundary that is still waiting, and sends the content of those boundaries as it becomes ready. The browser hydrates the shell while the rest is still arriving, so the page is interactive before its slow parts are there.

A boundary is either a `loading.tsx` file, which wraps the page below its folder in `<Suspense fallback={<Loading />}>`, or a `<Suspense>` you write in a component. A page waits inside a boundary for two things: a `Page.Defer` value it reads with `use()`, and code that loads late (`React.lazy`, `dynamic()`).

A boundary whose content is ready when the shell goes out is written in place, at its position in the HTML, however large it is. So a page that waits on nothing renders complete, and shows without JavaScript. Only what is still waiting comes later, after the shell, with a small inline script that puts it in place of the fallback. Without JavaScript that script does not run, and the fallback stays. ([ADR 0012](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/decisions/0012-streamed-documents-and-deferred-values.md) explains the choice.)

Under a hash-based Content-Security-Policy, which output-cached pages need, those inline scripts are blocked, so such pages must not stream. See [security](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/security.md#content-security-policy).

## Slow data with Page.Defer

`Page.Defer` puts a value in the props that is still being computed. The page renders without waiting for it, and the value streams to the page when it is ready, like a slow `fetch` behind a Suspense boundary in a Next.js server component. Use it for parts of a page that can come a moment later: comments, an activity feed, recommendations.

```csharp
public sealed record PostProps(PostDetail Post, Deferred<IReadOnlyList<PostSummary>> Related);

app.MapPageLoader("/blog/[slug]", (string slug, PostStore store, HttpContext http) =>
    store.Find(slug) is { } post
        ? Page.Props(new PostProps(
            new PostDetail(post.Slug, post.Title, post.Body, post.Tags, post.PublishedOn),
            Page.Defer(RelatedAsync(store, slug, http.RequestAborted))))
        : Page.NotFound());
```

The prop's type is `Deferred<T>`. In the generated types it is a `deferred()` schema, which `definePage` parses into a thenable. Read it with React's `use()` inside a Suspense boundary:

```tsx
import { definePage } from 'netjes';
import { Suspense, use } from 'react';
import { type PostSummary, pages } from '../../../generated/netjes.ts';

function Related({ related }: { related: PromiseLike<PostSummary[]> }) {
  const posts = use(related);
  return <ul>{posts.map((post) => <li key={post.slug}>{post.title}</li>)}</ul>;
}

export default definePage(pages['/blog/[slug]'], function Post({ post, related }) {
  return (
    <article>
      <h1>{post.title}</h1>
      <Suspense fallback={<p>Finding related posts…</p>}>
        <Related related={related} />
      </Suspense>
    </article>
  );
});
```

The value is validated against its schema when it arrives. `deferred(schema)` from `netjes/zod` builds the same schema by hand.

### The two overloads

| Overload | When the work starts | Services |
|---|---|---|
| `Page.Defer(Task<T> task)` | When you call it: you hand over a task that is already running. | Whatever the task captured, in the request's own scope. |
| `Page.Defer(Func<IServiceProvider, Task<T>> load)` | Once the page's payload is written, after the loaders have finished. | A DI scope of its own, disposed when the value is done. |

A task that uses a scoped service runs at the same time as the rest of the request, and an EF Core `DbContext` must not be used by two operations at once. The TaskBoard example creates a context of its own for the deferred work, from an `IDbContextFactory<TaskBoardDb>`:

```csharp
var activity = Page.Defer(ActivityAsync(contexts, access.ProjectId, number, http.RequestAborted));

static async Task<IReadOnlyList<ActivityItem>> ActivityAsync(
    IDbContextFactory<TaskBoardDb> contexts, Guid projectId, int number, CancellationToken cancellationToken)
{
    await using var db = await contexts.CreateDbContextAsync(cancellationToken);
    return await db.Activity
        .Where(a => a.ProjectId == projectId && a.TaskNumber == number)
        .OrderByDescending(a => a.At)
        .Take(30)
        .Select(a => new ActivityItem(a.Id, a.Summary, a.Actor.Name, a.At))
        .ToListAsync(cancellationToken);
}
```

The second overload does the same without the factory: it hands the work a service provider of its own scope, so the `TaskBoardDb` it resolves is not the one the loaders use.

```csharp
var activity = Page.Defer(services => ActivityAsync(
    services.GetRequiredService<TaskBoardDb>(), access.ProjectId, number, http.RequestAborted));

static async Task<IReadOnlyList<ActivityItem>> ActivityAsync(
    TaskBoardDb db, Guid projectId, int number, CancellationToken cancellationToken) =>
    await db.Activity
        .Where(a => a.ProjectId == projectId && a.TaskNumber == number)
        .OrderByDescending(a => a.At)
        .Take(30)
        .Select(a => new ActivityItem(a.Id, a.Summary, a.Actor.Name, a.At))
        .ToListAsync(cancellationToken);
```

`Page.Defer` works in the props of pages and layouts, anywhere in the props object, and in any number.

### On the wire

- A document carries a placeholder for each value, and the value follows in the same response, as a small inline script, once it is ready.
- A client navigation gets NDJSON instead of JSON: the payload on the first line, then one line per value as it completes.

A value that throws, or has not arrived when `StreamTimeout` runs out, rejects on the client, and `use()` throws it to the nearest `error.tsx`. In production the message is "Something went wrong"; in development it is the exception's message. The failure is logged as a warning (category `Netjes.Deferred`).

## Complete documents

Some readers get the whole document at once, with every boundary in place and no fallbacks:

- Crawlers and link previews, whose `User-Agent` matches `NetjesOptions.CrawlerUserAgents` (a case-insensitive regular expression; the default covers search engine bots, social previews, Lighthouse and the like).
- Every document, when `NetjesOptions.StreamDocuments` is `false`.
- `netjes export`, which writes complete documents to files (see [static export](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/static-export.md)).

The response then starts once every deferred value has arrived, up to `StreamTimeout`. The values still follow as inline scripts, for the browser to hydrate what they rendered. Client navigations stream their NDJSON either way.

## When no sidecar is ready

In production, a document request that finds no Node process ready (they have all crashed and are restarting) does not wait for one. Loaders and authorization run as usual and the response has the status it would have had, but .NET writes the document itself: a head with the stylesheets, the client entry and the CSP nonce, the `<title>`, description and robots from the loader's `PageMetadata`, and a body with only the page payload. The browser renders the page instead of hydrating it, and `Page.Defer` values stream in after it as usual. ([ADR 0013](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/decisions/0013-client-rendered-fallback.md) has the reasoning.)

- Each such document logs a warning, `No Node sidecar was ready to render {Route} ({Path}); the page was sent for the browser to render.`, and adds one to the `netjes.sidecar.fallbacks` counter on the `Netjes` meter, tagged `netjes.route`.
- It is never stored in the output cache, and it goes out with `Cache-Control: no-store` in place of any header the page set, and without the headers a CDN reads ahead of `Cache-Control` (`CDN-Cache-Control`, `Surrogate-Control` and the others listed in [caching](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/caching.md#cdns-and-proxies)), so no browser, and no CDN that goes by the response's headers, keeps it once the processes are back.
- Visitors without JavaScript, and crawlers and link previews that run none, get an empty page with the title, description and robots from C#. Layout title templates, and the metadata that page and layout files export, apply once the page renders.
- The health check reports Unhealthy while it lasts.
- A render that reached a process and failed there, or timed out, still gets the error page.
- Development never falls back, since its process also runs the Vite dev server the browser loads from, and neither does `netjes export`.

`NetjesOptions.ClientRenderFallback = false` (`Netjes__ClientRenderFallback=false`) turns it off: such a request then waits for a restart, up to `RenderTimeout` (`StreamTimeout` for a complete document), and gets the error page if none comes.

## Components that load late or only in the browser

`dynamic()` loads a component's module on demand, in a chunk of its own, like `next/dynamic`:

```tsx
import { dynamic } from 'netjes';

const Chart = dynamic(() => import('./Chart.tsx'), { loading: Spinner });
const Map = dynamic(() => import('./Map.tsx'), { ssr: false, loading: Spinner });
```

With `ssr` (the default), the component renders on the server like any other; on a page the browser has not loaded the chunk for yet, it suspends until the module is there. With `ssr: false`, the server and the first render in the browser show `loading`, and the component renders after hydration: use it for code that needs `window` or a browser-only library.

`clientOnly(Component, { fallback })` renders an existing component only in the browser, after hydration, and `fallback` (default nothing) on the server and before that.

Both are in the [React API reference](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/reference/react-api.md).

## Error pages

If something fails while Netjes serves a page, it renders the nearest boundary file instead, with the response's status:

- An exception in a loader, in an action without JavaScript, or in the React render: the nearest `error.tsx` above the segment that failed, inside the layouts above it, with status 500 (or the status of a `BadHttpRequestException`). A layout loader that throws renders the boundary above its own layout.
- `Page.NotFound()`, `Page.Forbidden()`, `Page.Unauthorized()`, and empty 401, 403 and 404 responses (from authorization, say): the nearest `not-found.tsx`, `forbidden.tsx` or `unauthorized.tsx`, else the error page. A user who fails a layout loader's `RequireAuthorization(...)` gets that section's own boundary (or the nearest above it) inside the layouts above the section, and the section's loader never runs.
- If the error page fails to render too: `app/global-error.tsx`, without any layout. If that is missing or fails as well: a plain HTML page with the status.

An `error.tsx` gets `{ error, reset }`, with the status as `error.status`. In production `error.message` is the status's reason phrase ("Internal Server Error"), so nothing about the exception reaches the browser. In development it is the exception's message, and the stack is there too: the JavaScript stack for a render that failed in the sidecar (`SsrRenderException.JsStack`), the .NET one otherwise. `NetjesOptions.IncludeErrorDetails` sets this either way. Both are plain text, without the terminal colour codes Vite puts in its errors, and the message can take several lines, such as the code frame Vite reports for a syntax error in a page: show it with `white-space: pre-wrap` (`whitespace-pre-wrap` in Tailwind CSS), as the built-in error page and the template's `error.tsx` do.

Every such failure is logged: unhandled exceptions as errors, bad requests as warnings (category `Netjes.Rendering.PageErrorMiddleware`). The [routing guide](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/routing.md) describes where each boundary file goes.

<!-- Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/caching.md -->

# Caching

This guide is for app developers who want pages served from a cache, or need to know what browsers and proxies keep. It covers the `Cache-Control` Netjes sends by default, `CachePage` on ASP.NET Core output caching, the rules that apply to a page under any output caching, revalidation, draft mode, and what to watch for with CDNs and cookies. The client's own cache of server state (TanStack Query) is in [data loading](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/data-loading.md).

## What browsers keep by default

Page responses, documents and client payloads alike, go out with `Cache-Control: no-store, private`, unless the page set the header itself or the output cache stores the response. That is what Next.js sends for its dynamic pages, and for the same reason: a page carries per-user data (shared props, an antiforgery token), and browsers show a page they kept on Back and Forward without asking the server again. A kept page would show a signed-in user's page on Back after they signed out.

Back past a full page load therefore fetches the page again, unless the browser's back/forward cache restores it (Chrome restores `no-store` pages while the site's cookies are unchanged). A page that should stay in the browser's cache sets its own `Cache-Control`, in its loader or an endpoint filter, and then can come back on Back after a sign-out.

The response that sets the antiforgery cookie, which is a visitor's first page, goes out with ASP.NET Core's own `Cache-Control: no-cache, no-store` and `Pragma: no-cache` instead, so no browser or proxy keeps it either. Later pages reuse that cookie and get the default.

Some responses always get `no-store` in place of the page's own header: draft pages and the redirects loaders return in draft mode (`no-store, private`), the [client-rendered fallback](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/rendering-and-streaming.md#when-no-sidecar-is-ready), and the page rendered again for a failed form post, which holds what was typed (`no-store`): a server action's post without JavaScript, and a page action's post with or without it. Server action answers and `/_netjes/antiforgery` go out `no-store` too. All of them also go out without the headers a CDN reads ahead of `Cache-Control` ([CDNs and proxies](#cdns-and-proxies)).

Static files are ASP.NET Core's: in production, the content-hashed files Vite writes under `/assets` are sent with `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable`, and the other files in `public/` with no `Cache-Control`.

## Output-cached pages

`CachePage` caches a page on ASP.NET Core output caching, like incremental static regeneration in Next.js: the page is rendered at most once per `duration` and served from the cache in between.

```csharp
builder.Services.AddOutputCache();
// ...
app.UseNetjes();
app.UseAuthentication();
app.UseAuthorization();
app.UseAntiforgery();
app.UseOutputCache(); // after UseNetjes and after authentication

app.MapPageLoader("/blog/[slug]", (string slug, PostStore store) => /* ... */)
    .CachePage(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30), "posts");
```

`CachePage(duration, params tags)` works on anything that takes endpoint conventions: a page loader, `MapPages()` for every file page, a group, or a minimal API that returns `Page.Render`.

The order in the pipeline matters:

- `UseOutputCache()` after `UseNetjes()`. Before it, the output cache runs before routing, so no endpoint's policy applies, `CachePage` included, and Netjes logs a warning naming the order.
- `UseOutputCache()` after `UseAuthentication()`, so the output cache can see who is signed in. ASP.NET Core's default policy neither serves nor stores a response for a signed-in user or a request with an `Authorization` header.

### What is stored

The output cache stores a page's response when:

- the request is a `GET` or `HEAD` without a signed-in user or an `Authorization` header,
- the status is 200 and the response sets no cookie,
- the document carries no CSP nonce (a stored nonce would be every visitor's; Netjes logs a warning once per page, see [security](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/security.md#content-security-policy)),
- and the request is not in draft mode, not the page rendered for a failed form post, and not the client-rendered fallback.

A render that is not stored is one visitor's page, and gets the default `no-store, private`. Netjes judges that when the response starts: a refusal the output cache makes later, such as for a body over its `MaximumBodySize`, leaves the response without `Cache-Control`. Stored responses carry no `Cache-Control` of their own.

### How entries are keyed

Each entry is keyed on:

- the scheme, the host, and the path and query string exactly as sent, case included. Loaders get route and query values as sent, so `/s/Ab` and `/s/aB` can be different pages, and each query string is a page of its own (`?tag=a&tag=b` and `?tag=b&tag=a` are two entries).
- whether it is a document or a client payload, and for a payload, which of the page's layouts the client already holds (it then leaves their props out).
- the client build. During a rolling deploy, instances on the old and the new build do not serve each other's entries.

The cache's size limit counts response bodies, not keys, and every host and query string makes a new entry. In production, pin `AllowedHosts` to your host names and size the cache:

```csharp
builder.Services.AddOutputCache(options => options.SizeLimit = 200 * 1024 * 1024); // bytes; ASP.NET Core's default is 100 MB
```

### What a stored page leaves out

A response the output cache may store carries no antiforgery token, since the stored copy would hand one visitor's token to everyone it is served to. Pages under `CachePage` never carry one. Before a server action call or a `<Form>` post, the client fetches a token from `/_netjes/antiforgery`, and again after each action or navigation, since signing in or out changes it. So forms on cached pages need JavaScript: without it the post has no token and is refused.

### Shared props and cookies

A stored entry is every visitor's, shared props included. Shared props and the loaders of cached pages must not depend on cookies or other per-visitor state. Shared props built from the signed-in user are fine, since signed-in users never get a cached page.

As a backstop, a render the output cache will store that reads `Request.Cookies` (draft mode's cookie aside) logs a warning once per page: the render was stored and will be served to every visitor. It is still stored, because refusing would turn caching off behind any middleware that reads a cookie on each request (cookie authentication, sessions, a cookie culture provider). Reads of the raw `Cookie` header are not seen. Read per-visitor values on the client, or leave the page uncached. `UseAuthentication()` placed after `UseOutputCache()` also triggers the warning.

### Under any output caching

The keys and rules above hold however a page is output-cached, not only with `CachePage`:

- `.CacheOutput()` plain, named (`.CacheOutput("pages")`) or built (`.CacheOutput(p => p.Expire(...))`),
- an `[OutputCache]` attribute on the loader,
- conventions on `MapPages()`,
- a base policy of the app (`options.AddBasePolicy(...)`).

The differences: under those, a response the output cache will not store keeps its antiforgery token, while `CachePage` pages never carry one. And an endpoint that is no page but renders one (a minimal API returning `Page.Render` or `Page.Redirect`) gets these keys only from `CachePage`. Under other output caching its pages are not stored, and Netjes logs a warning once per endpoint.

A policy's own keys still add to these: `SetVaryByQuery("page")` cannot narrow the key, since the query string as sent is part of it already. ([ADR 0016](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/decisions/0016-page-cache-rules-under-any-output-caching.md) explains why the rules apply under every policy.)

## Revalidating

A server action evicts cached pages with `.Revalidate(tags)` or `.RevalidatePath(paths)` on its result. The client then loads the page on screen again:

```csharp
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc; // [FromForm]

app.MapAction("posts.publish", async ([FromForm] PublishPost input, PostStore posts) =>
{
    await posts.PublishAsync(input.Slug);
    return ServerAction.Ok().Revalidate("posts").RevalidatePath($"/blog/{input.Slug}");
});
```

- `Revalidate(tags)` evicts every entry tagged with one of these tags: the tags given to `CachePage(duration, tags)`, or by any other output-cache policy.
- `RevalidatePath(paths)` evicts the entries of each path, documents and payloads, with any query string. The path is matched without regard to case or a trailing slash, and without the base path (`/blog/hello`, not `/docs/blog/hello` under `UsePathBase("/docs")`).

Outside actions (a webhook from your CMS, a background job), inject `IPageCache`:

```csharp
app.MapPost("/webhooks/cms", async (CmsEvent change, IPageCache cache) =>
{
    await cache.RevalidatePathAsync($"/blog/{change.Slug}");
    await cache.RevalidateTagAsync("posts");
    return Results.NoContent();
}).RequireAuthorization("cms");
```

Without output caching both do nothing. Eviction is the app's own: with several instances, it reaches the others only through a store they share (see [deployment](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/deployment.md#several-instances)), and it never reaches a CDN.

## Draft mode

Draft mode lets an editor see unpublished content on pages that are otherwise cached, like Next.js's `draftMode()`. Turn it on from an endpoint you protect, and read it in loaders with `IDraftMode`:

```csharp
app.MapGet("/preview/on", (IDraftMode draft) =>
    {
        draft.Enable();
        return Results.LocalRedirect("/");
    })
    .RequireAuthorization("editors");

app.MapGet("/preview/off", (IDraftMode draft) =>
{
    draft.Disable();
    return Results.LocalRedirect("/");
});

app.MapPageLoader("/blog/[slug]", (string slug, IDraftMode draft, PostStore posts) =>
        posts.Find(slug, includeDrafts: draft.IsEnabled) is { } post ? Page.Props(new PostProps(post)) : Page.NotFound())
    .CachePage(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5));
```

- `Enable()` sets a cookie signed with ASP.NET Core Data Protection that lasts `NetjesOptions.DraftModeDuration` (one hour). It is `HttpOnly`, and outside Development `SameSite=None; Secure`, so a CMS on another site can show the preview in a frame (allow that with `SecurityHeaders.DraftFrameAncestors`, see [security](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/security.md#security-headers)).
- While it is on, output caching is bypassed for that visitor under any policy: nothing is looked up, and nothing that answers a draft request is stored, a redirect a loader returns included. Each draft request has a cache key of its own, so editors previewing a page at once do not wait for each other.
- Draft pages go out `Cache-Control: no-store, private`, without the headers a CDN reads ahead of it ([CDNs and proxies](#cdns-and-proxies)). So does a redirect a page or layout loader returns while draft mode is on, since where a draft leads (an unpublished slug, say) is draft content too.
- In React, `useDraftMode()` returns `{ isEnabled }`, for a "Leave preview" banner.
- The image endpoint is the exception: an image is the same for editors and visitors, so editors share its cache.

## CDNs and proxies

Netjes sends no CDN headers. A stored page goes out without `Cache-Control`, so a CDN in front of the app keeps it only under rules you give the CDN, and `Revalidate` and `RevalidatePath` evict the app's own output cache only.

Page responses carry `Vary: X-Netjes-Data, X-Netjes-Segments`: the same URL answers with a document or a client payload, and a payload depends on the layouts the client holds. A cache that keeps pages has to keep those apart, or pass every request with `X-Netjes-Data` through to the app.

Where Netjes sends `no-store` whatever the page set (draft pages and draft redirects, the client-rendered fallback, the page for a failed form post, action answers and antiforgery tokens), it also removes the headers a CDN or proxy reads ahead of `Cache-Control`, in any casing: `CDN-Cache-Control` and any other header whose name ends in `-Cache-Control` (a CDN's own, such as `Cloudflare-CDN-Cache-Control`), `Surrogate-Control`, `Edge-Control` and `X-Accel-Expires`. A CDN that reads one of them would otherwise keep a draft, or go on serving the fallback, whatever `Cache-Control` says. Netjes does this when it renders the response and again as the response starts, after the `Response.OnStarting` callbacks of loaders, actions and middleware registered after `UseNetjes`. A callback of middleware ahead of `UseNetjes` runs after Netjes's, so what it adds still goes out. On every other response, the headers a page sets go out as they are ([ADR 0019](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/decisions/0019-forced-no-store-removes-cdn-cache-headers.md)).

## Images

The `<Image>` endpoint (`/_netjes/image`) is output-cached whenever the app uses output caching, for signed-in visitors too, and sends long-lived `Cache-Control` and an `ETag`. See [images](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/images.md).

<!-- Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/metadata.md -->

# Metadata

This guide is for app developers. It covers what goes in a page's `<head>`: titles, descriptions, Open Graph and Twitter tags, canonical and alternate links, from page and layout files or from a C# loader. It also covers `sitemap.xml` and `robots.txt`, and loading third-party scripts with `<Script>`. The API follows the Next.js Metadata API.

## Titles and tags from page files

A page or a layout exports `metadata`:

```tsx
// app/layout.tsx
import type { Metadata } from 'netjes';

export const metadata: Metadata = {
  title: { default: 'Netjes Blog', template: '%s · Netjes Blog' },
  openGraph: { siteName: 'Netjes Blog', type: 'website' },
};
```

```tsx
// app/guestbook/page.tsx
export const metadata: Metadata = { title: 'Guestbook' }; // <title>Guestbook · Netjes Blog</title>
```

Netjes merges the metadata of the layouts above a page (outermost first), then the page's own, then what the page's C# loader sent, and writes the result as tags that React puts in the head. Each later one replaces what the earlier ones set, field by field: `openGraph`, `twitter`, `alternates`, `icons` and `other` are merged key by key, everything else is replaced. On a client navigation the tags change with the page.

### Titles

`title` is a string, or an object:

| Title | Effect |
|---|---|
| `'Guestbook'` | Goes through the nearest `template` from a layout above. |
| `{ template: '%s · Docs' }` | In a layout: `%s` is replaced by the title of each page below it. |
| `{ default: 'Netjes Blog' }` | In a layout: the title of pages below it that set none. A layout's own default does not go through its own template, only through templates from layouts above it. |
| `{ absolute: 'Home' }` | Used as it is, skipping every template. |

The Blog's docs layout nests a template inside the root one: `export const metadata: Metadata = { title: { template: '%s · Docs · Netjes Blog' } };` makes a docs page's title `Routing · Docs · Netjes Blog`.

### Fields

| Field | Written as |
|---|---|
| `title` | `<title>` |
| `description` | `<meta name="description">` |
| `keywords` | `<meta name="keywords">`, joined with commas |
| `authors: [{ name, url? }]` | `<meta name="author">` per author (the name) |
| `robots` | `<meta name="robots">`: a string as it is, or `{ index, follow }` as `index, follow`, `noindex, nofollow` and so on |
| `alternates.canonical` | `<link rel="canonical">` |
| `alternates.languages: { 'nl': '/nl' }` | `<link rel="alternate" hreflang>` per language |
| `openGraph` | `og:title`, `og:description`, `og:url`, `og:site_name`, `og:type`, `og:locale`, and `og:image` per image, each followed by its `og:image:width`, `og:image:height` and `og:image:alt` when set |
| `twitter` | `twitter:card`, `twitter:site`, `twitter:creator`, `twitter:title`, `twitter:description`, and `twitter:image` per image, each followed by its `twitter:image:alt` when set |
| `icons: { icon, apple }` | `<link rel="icon">`, `<link rel="apple-touch-icon">` |
| `themeColor` | `<meta name="theme-color">` |
| `other: { name: content }` | `<meta name content>` per entry |

An image's `alt` is written only when it is not empty, and its `width` and `height` only when they are above zero. URLs are written as given, so give crawlers absolute image URLs: under a [base path](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/routing.md#base-path), an icon in `public/` needs the base path in front (`useBasePath()` in a layout that renders the `<link>` itself).

### Open Graph and Twitter

`openGraph.images` and `twitter.images` take one image or an array of them, as in Next.js: each is a URL, as a string or a `URL`, or `{ url, width, height, alt }` with the details optional. An empty entry, or an image with an empty URL, is left out.

Once the layouts', the page's and the C# metadata are merged, the link preview tags that are not set fill in as they do in Next.js:

- With `openGraph` metadata, `og:title` and `og:description` take the page's title and description where `openGraph` sets none.
- With `openGraph` or `twitter` metadata, `twitter:title`, `twitter:description` and the `twitter:image` tags take the Open Graph title, description and images that `twitter` does not set, and the page's title and description where there is no Open Graph one either. A title taken this way does not go through a template again: an Open Graph title is used as set, the page's title as its layouts' templates made it.
- Where `twitter` sets no `card`, `twitter:card` is `summary_large_image` when `twitter.images` has an image and `summary` when it has none; with no `twitter` metadata at all, the Open Graph images decide. So `twitter: { site: '@acme' }` next to Open Graph images writes a `summary` card with those images: set `card: 'summary_large_image'` for the large one.

An empty title or description counts as not set, so it takes the fallback, and no `og:` or `twitter:` title or description tag is written empty. An empty `twitter.images` list does count as set: it keeps the Open Graph images out of the Twitter tags, and the card is `summary` unless `twitter` sets one.

### Special pages

`not-found.tsx`, `error.tsx`, `forbidden.tsx` and `unauthorized.tsx` export `metadata` too, and the layouts' title templates apply to them. An `error.tsx`'s metadata applies when the server renders it; an error caught in the browser keeps the page's title.

### `<title>` and `<meta>` elements

React 19 hoists `<title>`, `<meta>` and `<link>` elements rendered anywhere into the head, so a component can render them itself. Below a layout that sets a title, use `metadata` instead: the layout's title is still written, so a `<title>` element makes a second one.

## Metadata from C#

For a title or description that depends on data, the loader sends it with `.WithMetadata(...)`, the counterpart of Next.js's `generateMetadata`:

```csharp
app.MapPageLoader("/blog", (string? tag, PostStore store) =>
    Page.Props(new BlogIndexProps(tag, store.Tags(), store.Posts(tag)))
        .WithMetadata(new PageMetadata { Title = tag is null ? "Blog" : $"Posts tagged {tag}" }));
```

It is merged over the files' metadata, so the layouts' title templates still apply: `Posts tagged dotnet · Netjes Blog`. `PageMetadata` has `Title`, `Description`, `Keywords`, `Robots` (`new PageMetadataRobots(Index: false)`), `Alternates` (`Canonical`, `Languages`), `OpenGraph` (`Title`, `Description`, `Url`, `SiteName`, `Type`, `Locale`, `Images`), `Twitter` (`Card`, `Site`, `Creator`, `Images`; each image is a `PageMetadataImage`, and a plain URL string converts to one), `ThemeColor` and `Other`. Icons and authors are set in the files only.

```csharp
.WithMetadata(new PageMetadata
{
    Title = post.Title,
    Description = post.Summary,
    Alternates = new PageMetadataAlternates(Canonical: $"https://blog.example/blog/{post.Slug}"),
    OpenGraph = new PageMetadataOpenGraph { Type = "article", Images = [new PageMetadataImage($"https://blog.example/img/{post.Slug}.png", 1200, 630, post.Title)] },
})
```

A layout loader's result can carry metadata too, but only the page loader's reaches the head.

If no Node sidecar is ready and the browser renders the page itself, the document Netjes writes has the title, description and robots from C# only; the layouts' templates and the files' metadata apply once the page has rendered ([Rendering and streaming](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/rendering-and-streaming.md)).

## The `lang` attribute

`<html lang>` is `NetjesOptions.Lang`, `en` by default. With [locale routing](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/routing.md#locales) it follows the request culture.

## Sitemap and robots

```csharp
var siteUrl = new Uri(app.Configuration["SiteUrl"] ?? "http://localhost:5080");
app.MapSitemap(siteUrl);
app.MapRobotsTxt(siteUrl);
app.MapPages();
```

`MapSitemap(siteUrl, cacheFor)` serves `/sitemap.xml`, the counterpart of `app/sitemap.ts`, from the route table:

- every page without parameters, and each dynamic page's URLs from its `.StaticParams(...)` ([Static export](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/static-export.md));
- not the pages that require authorization, their own or through a fallback policy, unless they are `.AllowAnonymous()`;
- not the pages marked `.ExcludeFromSitemap()`.

URLs are absolute, under `siteUrl` and the app's base path, with the base path percent-encoded as a URL path. The list of pages is built at most once per `cacheFor` (an hour by default), so `StaticParams` does not run on every request. The XML is kept for the first eight base paths it is requested under in each `cacheFor`, which is one in a normal app. When the base path can come from a client (an `X-Forwarded-Prefix` the app accepts from untrusted addresses), any further one is built from the kept list on each request instead. Under a base path longer than 256 characters as the XML writes it (percent-encoded, with each `&` as `&amp;`), `/sitemap.xml` is not found (404, `Cache-Control: no-store`, logged at debug level) and nothing is built: every URL would repeat the base path, so one small request could ask for a large answer. The sitemap itself is sent with `Cache-Control: public, max-age` set to `cacheFor`.

`MapRobotsTxt(siteUrl, disallow)` serves `/robots.txt`: `Disallow` for each path given (or `Allow: /` when none is), and a `Sitemap:` line with the URL `MapSitemap` is served at: `/sitemap.xml` under `siteUrl` and the app's base path. Both endpoints allow anonymous requests.

Crawlers read `robots.txt` only at the root of the host. Under a base path, serve the root file from whatever answers the root, with the `Sitemap:` line from the app's own `robots.txt`. The `disallow` paths are written as given, so include the base path in them.

Leave `/_netjes/` out of `disallow`. `<Image>` serves every image through `/_netjes/image`, so a crawler that may not fetch it cannot index your images. The other endpoints there take posts (server actions and web vitals) or hand out an antiforgery token, which a crawler has no use for.

## Third-party scripts: `<Script>`

`<Script>` loads a script without blocking the page, like `next/script`. It renders nothing where it stands; each script is added to the document once, by its `id` or `src`, however many components render it.

```tsx
import { Script } from 'netjes';

<Script src="https://analytics.example/script.js" strategy="lazyOnload" onLoad={() => console.log('loaded')} />

<Script id="consent-defaults">{`window.dataLayer = window.dataLayer || [];`}</Script>
```

| `strategy` | When the script runs |
|---|---|
| `afterInteractive` (default) | Added once the page has hydrated. |
| `lazyOnload` | Added after the page's `load` event, when the browser is idle. |
| `beforeInteractive` | Written into the server-rendered head, before the page's own scripts. External scripts only; an inline one is added after hydration. |

- Inline code goes in as the children, with an `id`, which a script without `src` needs.
- `onLoad` and `onError` are called once the script has loaded or failed, also for a component that renders a script another one added before it.
- Other attributes, such as `integrity`, `crossOrigin` or `data-*`, are set on the element.
- Under a [Content-Security-Policy](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/security.md) with a nonce, `<Script>` puts the page's nonce on the script. For an inline script of your own, read it with `useNonce()`.

<!-- Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/images.md -->

# Images

This guide is for app developers. It covers the `<Image>` component and the `/_netjes/image` endpoint behind it, the counterparts of `next/image` and `/_next/image`: where images may come from, the widths and qualities served, the formats, the limits that keep the endpoint safe under load, and how images are resized, through an `IImageProcessor` such as the optional SkiaSharp package ([ADR 0008](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/decisions/0008-pluggable-image-processing.md)).

## Showing an image

```tsx
import { Image } from 'netjes';

{/* A fixed size: a 1x and a 2x copy. */}
<Image src="/img/avatar.png" width={64} height={64} alt="Ada Lovelace" />

{/* Responsive: every configured width, and the browser picks by `sizes`. Above the fold, so `priority`. */}
<Image
  src="/hero.png"
  width={1600}
  height={800}
  sizes="(max-width: 64rem) 100vw, 64rem"
  priority
  alt="Gradient in the blog's accent colours"
  className="h-auto w-full"
/>
```

`<Image>` renders an `<img>` with its `width` and `height`, so the page keeps the space and does not shift as it loads. It loads lazily and decodes asynchronously, and its `srcset` points at resized copies from the endpoint:

- Without `sizes`, a fixed-size image gets two candidates: the smallest configured width that covers `width`, as `1x`, and the one that covers twice that, as `2x`.
- With `sizes`, it gets every configured width as a `w` candidate, and the browser picks one by the layout.
- `priority` loads it eagerly with high fetch priority and preloads it from the document head. Use it for the image a visitor sees first.
- `quality` (1–100, default 75) is rounded to the nearest quality the server accepts.
- `unoptimized` serves `src` as it is. SVGs, `data:` URLs and `blob:` URLs are always served as they are.

`src` is a path in `public/` (`/img/hero.png`) or a URL on an allowed remote host. `alt` is required; give `""` for a decorative image. Every other `<img>` attribute, such as `className` or `style`, passes through. Under a [base path](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/routing.md#base-path), write `src` as if the app were at the root.

The configured widths, qualities and the endpoint's path reach the component with the first document, so the server's configuration is the only one. A static host has no image endpoint, so pages from `netjes export` need `unoptimized` on their images ([Static export](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/static-export.md#what-cannot-be-exported)).

## The image endpoint

`app.MapPages()` maps `GET /_netjes/image?url=…&w=…&q=…`. It reads the source, hands it to the registered `IImageProcessor` with the width, quality and an output format the browser accepts, and answers with the result:

- `Cache-Control: public, max-age=…` for `CacheDuration` (7 days), an `ETag` (a matching `If-None-Match` gets 304), and `Vary: Accept`.
- `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` and `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; style-src 'unsafe-inline'; sandbox;`, so an image opened on its own, an SVG above all, runs no script.

If the app uses output caching (`AddOutputCache()` and `UseOutputCache()`), the endpoint's answers are cached: keyed by the width, the quality, the image as it is fetched and the negotiated format, not by the `Host` header. Requests with an `Authorization` header or a signed-in user are cached too, unlike under ASP.NET Core's default policy, since an image from `public/` or an allowed host is the same for everyone. Editors in draft mode share this cache. Serve private images from an endpoint of your own.

Without an image processor the endpoint serves the original bytes, cached as above. `Netjes:Images:Path` moves the endpoint; it is used with one leading slash and none trailing, and other spellings of it get 400.

## Where images come from

**Local images** come from `public/` in development and from the client build in production, where Vite has copied `public/`. A local `url` must be a plain path:

- no query, no fragment, no `.`, `..` or empty segments, and no backslash;
- spelled as its file is stored, case included. On Windows and macOS, `/img/HERO.png` for `hero.png` gets 400, and so do an 8.3 short name, a segment with a trailing dot or space, and an accented name in another Unicode form.

This keeps one cache entry per image and size. The endpoint lists a path's directories the first time the path is asked for, then remembers it (up to 4096 paths, after which it starts over). A file renamed while the app runs is still served under its old spelling, where the file system still opens it that way, until then or until the app restarts.

**Remote images** come only from the hosts in `Netjes:Images:RemoteHosts`:

```json
{
  "Netjes": {
    "Images": {
      "RemoteHosts": ["images.example.com", "*.cdn.example.com"]
    }
  }
}
```

- `images.example.com` allows that host; `*.example.com` allows its subdomains, not `example.com` itself.
- Over https only, unless `RemoteRequireHttps` is `false`, and on the scheme's default port, unless `RemotePorts` lists another.
- Redirects are never followed: a remote host that redirects gets 502.
- The host's address must be public. Loopback, private, link-local (`169.254.169.254`, where cloud metadata services live), shared and unique-local addresses are refused after DNS resolution, so an allowed name pointed at an internal service is never reached. An IPv6 address that carries an IPv4 one (IPv4-mapped, IPv4-compatible, NAT64 on `64:ff9b::/96` or a `/96` inside `64:ff9b:1::/48`, 6to4 on `2002::/16`) is judged by the IPv4 address inside, and Teredo is refused. A NAT64 prefix of your own network, or another RFC 6052 layout, cannot be recognised from the address: where DNS64 makes those, restrict the app's egress at the network as well.
- Fetches never use a proxy: `HTTP_PROXY` and `HTTPS_PROXY` are ignored, because through a proxy the address check would see the proxy. Where all egress must go through a proxy, remote images fail with 502 or 504; allow the app direct egress to its `RemoteHosts`, or serve those images from `public/`.
- The fetch has `RemoteTimeout` (10 seconds) for its headers and body together.

A remote URL is cached as it is fetched: host lower-cased, default port, dot segments and fragment dropped. Its path and query string are sent upstream as written, so `//a.png`, `/A.png` or a trailing `?` may be one image to the host and still be separate entries here. Allow only hosts you trust.

## Widths, qualities and formats

The endpoint serves only the widths in `Netjes:Images:Widths`, by default Next.js's device and image sizes: 16, 32, 48, 64, 96, 128, 256, 384, 640, 750, 828, 1080, 1200, 1920, 2048 and 3840. It accepts `DefaultQuality` (75) and the qualities in `Qualities` (by default only 75). A width or quality it does not serve, or one written with leading zeros (`w=0640`), gets 400. Configured lists replace the defaults:

```json
{
  "Netjes": {
    "Images": {
      "Widths": [320, 640, 1280, 1920],
      "Qualities": [50, 75, 90]
    }
  }
}
```

The endpoint goes by a source's bytes, not its file extension or `Content-Type`: it serves PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP and AVIF, and SVG when `AllowSvg` is on (it is off by default, because SVG can carry script; SVGs are served unprocessed). Anything else is refused, 400 for a local file and 502 for a remote one, and an image goes out typed as what its bytes are. The output format is the first of the processor's formats that the request's `Accept` header names, or the source's own format.

## Limits

| Option | Default | What it limits |
|---|---|---|
| `MaxSourceBytes` | 20 MB | The largest source read, local (400) or remote (502). |
| `MaxConcurrency` | one per CPU | Images read and processed at once. A request takes its slot before it reads the source. |
| `MaxRemoteFetches` | 16 | Remote images fetched at once, in slots of their own, so a slow host cannot hold up local images. A fetch keeps its slot until its image is processed. |
| `MaxQueue` | 1000 | Requests that may wait for a slot, in each of the two pools. More get 503 with `Retry-After`. |
| `RemoteTimeout` | 10 s | A remote fetch, headers and body together (then 504). |

Peak memory is about `MaxConcurrency` × (2 × `MaxSourceBytes` + 4 bytes × the processor's `MaxPixels`) + `MaxRemoteFetches` × `MaxSourceBytes`, so lower these in a small container. If most images are remote and their hosts are slow, raise `MaxRemoteFetches` rather than `MaxConcurrency`: a fetch waits on the network, while each processing slot can take a CPU and the memory of a decoded image.

| Status | When |
|---|---|
| 400 | A bad or non-canonical query, a width or quality not served, a host or port not allowed, a local file that is not a served image, is spelled otherwise than stored or is too large, or a local image the processor refuses. The body says which. |
| 404 | No such local file. |
| 502 | A remote image that is refused: a redirect, an error status, a non-public address, not an allowed image, too large, or refused by the processor. |
| 503 | The queue is full; `Retry-After` says when to try again. |
| 504 | A remote fetch took longer than `RemoteTimeout`. |

Under `UsePathBase` the endpoint answers with and without the base path, so each image can have two cache entries. Size the output cache (`SizeLimit`) for the images it holds as well as the pages ([Caching](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/caching.md)).

## Resizing with SkiaSharp

Without a processor, images are served as they are. The `Netjes.Images.SkiaSharp` package resizes them and encodes WebP:

```bash
dotnet add package Netjes.Images.SkiaSharp
```

```csharp
builder.Services.AddNetjes();
builder.Services.AddNetjesSkiaImages(o => o.MaxPixels = 25_000_000);
```

`AddNetjesSkiaImages` registers `SkiaImageProcessor`, before or after `AddNetjes()`. It:

- resizes to the requested width, never larger than the source, and applies the EXIF orientation;
- encodes WebP when the browser accepts it, and the source's own format otherwise;
- decodes large JPEGs at a reduced size;
- refuses an image whose header declares more than `MaxPixels` pixels (default 40 million, about 160 MB decoded) before decoding it, since a file of a few kilobytes can claim 40000×40000;
- decodes `MaxConcurrency` images at once (default one per CPU). `Netjes:Images:MaxConcurrency` limits the whole endpoint, reading included.

It decodes PNG, JPEG and WebP only, and only bytes that start with the declared format's signature, so no other codec SkiaSharp bundles (BMP, ICO and the rest) parses them, even when your own code calls the processor. GIFs (which may be animated) and AVIFs pass through unchanged. An image it cannot decode is refused, not passed through.

SkiaSharp's native codecs parse whatever a file in `public/` or an allowed host holds, so keep SkiaSharp current. If SkiaSharp ships a security update before `Netjes.Images.SkiaSharp` moves to it, add package references to the newer `SkiaSharp` and `SkiaSharp.NativeAssets.Linux.NoDependencies` yourself.

## Writing an image processor

Register your own `IImageProcessor` to resize with another library:

```csharp
public sealed class MyImageProcessor : IImageProcessor
{
    public IReadOnlyList<string> OutputFormats => ["image/webp", "image/jpeg"];

    public ValueTask<ProcessedImage> ProcessAsync(ImageSource source, ImageTransform transform, CancellationToken cancellationToken)
    {
        // source.Content: the bytes; source.ContentType: what they are (image/png, image/jpeg, image/gif, image/webp, image/avif).
        // transform.Width: a configured width; transform.Quality: 1-100; transform.Format: one of OutputFormats, or null for the source's.
        if (TooLarge(source))
        {
            throw new ImageRejectedException("The image has too many pixels.");
        }

        return ValueTask.FromResult(new ProcessedImage(Resize(source, transform), transform.Format ?? source.ContentType));
    }
}

builder.Services.AddSingleton<IImageProcessor, MyImageProcessor>();
```

- `OutputFormats` lists the formats it can encode, preferred first. The endpoint passes one the browser names in `Accept`, or `null` to keep the source's.
- `source.ContentType` is the format the bytes are, whatever the file's extension or the remote `Content-Type` said.
- Do not upscale past the source.
- Throwing `ImageRejectedException` answers with its message: 400 for a local image, 502 for a remote one.

All of the endpoint's options are listed in [Options](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/reference/options.md).

<!-- Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/static-export.md -->

# Static export

This guide is for app developers who want to publish a Netjes app, or part of one, as static files on a host without .NET: what `netjes export` writes, how dynamic pages list their URLs, what cannot be exported, and how exported pages behave in the browser, Content-Security-Policy included. It is the counterpart of Next.js's `output: 'export'`. The command's options are in the [CLI reference](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/reference/cli.md#netjes-export).

## What the export does

```bash
npx netjes export          # builds, then writes out/
npx netjes export site     # into site/ instead
npx netjes export --no-build
```

`netjes export` builds the app (as `netjes build` does), runs it once in Production, and requests every page through it over HTTP: the same pipeline a visitor hits, so loaders, layout loaders, middleware and output caching apply as usual. It writes:

- `out/index.html` for `/`, and `out/<path>/index.html` for every other page,
- `out/404.html`, the not-found page,
- a copy of the client build (`dist/client`, without Vite's `.vite/` folder).

As with Next.js, the loaders run once, at export time. The pages then hydrate in the browser as usual.

## Dynamic pages: StaticParams

A page with route parameters is exported once for each set of values its loader lists with `.StaticParams(...)`, like `generateStaticParams`:

```csharp
app.MapPageLoader("/blog/[slug]", (string slug, PostStore store) => /* ... */)
    .StaticParams<PostStore>(store => store.All.Select(post => new { slug = post.Slug }));

app.MapPageLoader("/docs/[...path]", (string path, DocsStore docs) => /* ... */)
    .StaticParams<DocsStore>(docs => docs.All.Select(doc => new { path = doc.Path.Split('/') }));
```

- One object per page, with a property for each route parameter. A catch-all takes an array of segments (or a string with `/` between them); an optional catch-all may leave it out.
- `.StaticParams<TService>(service => ...)` resolves the service for you; `.StaticParams(services => ...)` takes the `IServiceProvider`, in a scope of its own.
- Each value becomes a directory name, so it must not be empty, `.` or `..`, or contain `/`, `\`, `:` or a NUL character. The export refuses it otherwise.
- `MapSitemap` uses the same lists for the dynamic pages in `sitemap.xml` (see [metadata](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/metadata.md)).

Every listed page must answer 200. A loader that returns `Page.NotFound()` for a listed value fails the export, naming the URL.

## What cannot be exported

`.ExcludeFromExport()` leaves a page out, on its loader, its page action or `MapPages()`:

```csharp
app.MapPageLoader("/guestbook", (GuestbookStore store) => /* ... */).ExcludeFromExport(); // needs a server
```

Without it, the export stops before it writes anything, naming each problem, when a page:

- is dynamic and has no `.StaticParams(...)`,
- has a page action (`MapPageAction`), since form posts need a server,
- requires authorization, through `RequireAuthorization()` on it or a layout loader above it, or through a fallback policy (unless the page is `.AllowAnonymous()`),
- would write the same file as another page on some file system: paths that differ only in case, Unicode normalisation or trailing dots and spaces, or a `.StaticParams` value that lands on another page's URL,
- has a path segment that Windows reserves for a device (`con`, `nul.txt`, `com1`).

Server actions, minimal APIs, `/_netjes/antiforgery`, web vitals collection and the image endpoint have no static counterpart: an exported page that calls them gets the static host's 404. `<Image>` points its `src` and `srcset` at the image endpoint, so give images on exported pages `unoptimized`, which uses the file as it is.

## Where the output goes

The output directory is replaced as a whole, so the export checks it first. It must be inside the app, and must not overlap `app/`, `public/`, `dist/` or the folder of the generated types. An existing directory is replaced only when it is empty or a previous export, which the export marks with a `.netjes-export` file.

## Redirects

A page whose loader returns `Page.Redirect(url)` is written as a small page that refreshes to the target, with a link to it, the target written exactly as the loader sent it. Other redirects fail the export, naming the URL:

- a redirect the page did not make itself: a login redirect, HTTPS redirection, a URL rewriter rule,
- one that points at the export server's own address (use a relative URL),
- a target that is neither a path on the site nor an http(s) URL,
- a target that starts with a quote, which a meta refresh would drop.

## In the browser

Exported pages carry no antiforgery token, since there is no server to check it. They hydrate as usual, and links and `router.push` work, but every navigation is a full page load: the client router asks for the next page's data, gets a static HTML file instead, and loads it as a document. Query strings reach no loader, since the loaders ran at export time. Assets are linked from the site root, so serve the export at the root of its host.

## Deferred values and Suspense

Each page is exported as a complete document, the one crawlers get (see [rendering](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/rendering-and-streaming.md#complete-documents)). The export waits for the page's `Page.Defer` values, up to `StreamTimeout`, and writes what they render in place of their Suspense fallback (`loading.tsx`, or a `<Suspense>` in the page), with no script to reveal it. So an exported page shows its deferred content without JavaScript, and under a static host's Content-Security-Policy that runs no inline script.

The values also follow in inline scripts, for the client to hydrate that content. Under a policy that blocks those scripts, the content shows on load but its boundary does not hydrate: the first update that renders the boundary again (a state change in the page around it) replaces it with the fallback, for good. Two ways out:

- keep `Page.Defer` out of exported pages that update around their deferred content, or
- list the scripts' hashes in the host's policy, next to the bootstrap's (see [security](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/security.md#content-security-policy)). In an exported file those scripts are fixed text, and change only when a value does, so their hashes change only when you export again with other data.

A value that fails, or misses `StreamTimeout`, leaves its fallback in the file, and the nearest `error.tsx` replaces it once JavaScript runs. The export logs a warning and still succeeds.

<!-- Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/security.md -->

# Security

This guide is for app developers putting a Netjes app in front of real users. It lists what Netjes does by default and what is left to you: the security headers, Content-Security-Policy, the antiforgery and origin checks on actions, request body limits, redirects, the image endpoint, the Node sidecar, the secret that signs layout keys, host names and HTTPS, and the development server. To report a vulnerability, follow [SECURITY.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/SECURITY.md).

## Defaults at a glance

| What | Default | Change it with |
|---|---|---|
| `X-Content-Type-Options`, `Referrer-Policy`, framing headers on documents | On | `Netjes:SecurityHeaders` |
| Content-Security-Policy | Off | `NetjesOptions.ContentSecurityPolicy` |
| Antiforgery token and same-origin check on server actions and page actions | On | `.DisableAntiforgery()` on a page action; `AllowedActionOrigins` |
| Server action body limit | 1 MB | `ActionBodySizeLimit`, `[RequestSizeLimit]` |
| Fields a failed form hands back | Only declared ones, never private ones | `PrivateFormFields` |
| `Cache-Control` on pages | `no-store, private` | Your own header; see [caching](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/caching.md) |
| Error details in error pages | Development only | `IncludeErrorDetails` |
| Remote images | None allowed | `Netjes:Images:RemoteHosts` |
| Layout key secret | Random per process | `SegmentKeySecret` |
| HSTS, HTTPS redirection, `AllowedHosts` | ASP.NET Core's; the template turns on HSTS and HTTPS redirection outside Development | ASP.NET Core |

## Security headers

Every HTML document Netjes renders (pages, not-found and error pages, the plain fallback error page) carries these, unless the app has set that header itself:

| Header | Value |
|---|---|
| `X-Content-Type-Options` | `nosniff` |
| `Referrer-Policy` | `strict-origin-when-cross-origin` |
| `X-Frame-Options` | `SAMEORIGIN`, unless the app decides about framing itself (below) |
| `Content-Security-Policy` | `frame-ancestors 'self'` added to `NetjesOptions.ContentSecurityPolicy` when you set one, likewise |

Client payloads (JSON) and static files get none of them.

Framing is the app's own once it sends `X-Frame-Options` itself, or has `frame-ancestors` in the Content-Security-Policy that goes out: its own header, or else `NetjesOptions.ContentSecurityPolicy`. Netjes then adds neither framing header, so nothing contradicts it. Browsers obey `frame-ancestors` over `X-Frame-Options`, which cannot name another site, so to let a partner frame your pages, send `frame-ancestors 'self' https://partner.example`. ASP.NET Core antiforgery adds `X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN` with each new token cookie; browsers ignore it next to `frame-ancestors`, and `AntiforgeryOptions.SuppressXFrameOptionsHeader` turns it off.

`NetjesOptions.SecurityHeaders` (`Netjes:SecurityHeaders`) has two settings:

- `Enabled = false` turns them all off. To preview the app in an editor's frame, such as VS Code's Simple Browser, set it in `appsettings.Development.json`, and turn off the header that antiforgery adds in code, since ASP.NET Core does not bind `AntiforgeryOptions` from configuration:

  ```json
  { "Netjes": { "SecurityHeaders": { "Enabled": false } } }
  ```

  ```csharp
  if (builder.Environment.IsDevelopment())
  {
      builder.Services.AddAntiforgery(o => o.SuppressXFrameOptionsHeader = true);
  }
  ```

- `DraftFrameAncestors = ["https://cms.example"]` lets those sites frame pages in [draft mode](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/caching.md#draft-mode), for a CMS that shows the preview in a frame. Draft documents then get `frame-ancestors 'self' https://cms.example` (in Netjes's own policy, or a header with only that directive) and keep `X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN`, which still holds if a middleware rewrites the policy without `frame-ancestors`. A browser without `frame-ancestors` support cannot show the preview. Published pages stay same-origin. It is ignored when the app sets its own `X-Frame-Options` or `Content-Security-Policy`, or has `frame-ancestors` in `ContentSecurityPolicy`; put the sites there instead. Each entry must be one CSP source, such as `https://cms.example` or `https://*.cms.example`; anything else stops the app at startup.

To send other headers, or other values on some pages, see [redirects, rewrites and headers](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/redirects-rewrites-headers.md#headers).

## Content-Security-Policy

Netjes sends no Content-Security-Policy until you set `NetjesOptions.ContentSecurityPolicy`. It then sets the header on every document, unless the app sent one itself, with `frame-ancestors 'self'` added when the policy has no `frame-ancestors`. There are two kinds of policy, and the choice depends on whether your pages are output-cached.

### Nonce-based

Put `{nonce}` where the per-request nonce goes:

```csharp
builder.Services.AddNetjes(options =>
    options.ContentSecurityPolicy = "script-src 'nonce-{nonce}' 'strict-dynamic'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'self'");
```

Netjes makes a nonce for each document and puts it on everything it renders: the module scripts and preloads, the stylesheets, the payload, the scripts that stream deferred values and reveal Suspense boundaries, and Vite's `csp-nonce` meta (for the styles Vite injects in development). `useNonce()` returns it for inline scripts or styles of your own, and `<Script>` uses it.

A document with a nonce is never stored in the output cache: a stored copy would give every visitor the same, readable nonce. Netjes renders such a page each time and logs a warning once per output-cached page. For cached pages, use a hash-based policy.

If you write the policy yourself, for example with a headers library, call `HttpContext.GetCspNonce()` for the request's nonce, and Netjes puts the same one on what it renders. The output cache rule applies to that nonce as well.

### Hash-based

A policy without `{nonce}` makes no nonce, so pages under it can be output-cached. It must allow the one inline script Netjes puts in every document's head, the bootstrap that collects streamed values, by its hash:

```csharp
options.ContentSecurityPolicy =
    "script-src 'self' 'sha256-FSjVV+FzmXP8KKrLKLdvst/5N/bEWSkde01XzpGKRgs='; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'self'";
```

That is the hash of the bootstrap in this version; a Netjes version that changes its text changes the hash. Inline `<Script>` code of your own needs its hash listed too.

No hash covers what streams after the shell: each script that delivers a `Page.Defer` value carries that value, and React's scripts that reveal Suspense boundaries name the boundaries of that render. A hash-based policy blocks both, so a page served under one must not stream: no `Page.Defer`, and no Suspense boundary still waiting when the shell goes out (lazy code under `loading.tsx` included). Pages from `netjes export` are the exception, since their scripts are fixed text; see [static export](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/static-export.md#deferred-values-and-suspense).

## Server actions and page actions

Every server action (`MapAction`) and page action (`MapPageAction`) needs a valid ASP.NET Core antiforgery token and a same-origin request. Put `app.UseAntiforgery()` in the pipeline, after authentication. `<Form>`, `useAction` and `serverAction()` send the token; pages that carry none (output-cached ones) fetch it from `/_netjes/antiforgery` first.

- A token the server refuses: a client call gets 400 with `X-Netjes-Antiforgery: invalid`, which no other response carries, and the client sends that call once more with a fresh token (no other 400 proves that the action did not run). A post without JavaScript gets the 400 error page.
- The origin check, like Next.js's, compares the request's `Origin` with its `Host`, and refuses a request the browser marks `Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site` whatever its origin: 403. `Origin: null` passes only when the browser also says `Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin`. `NetjesOptions.AllowedActionOrigins` lists more origins, for a same-site origin such as a sibling subdomain; a cross-site post is refused even when its origin is listed.
- Behind a proxy that rewrites `Host`, every action fails the origin check until the app sees its public host. Use `UseForwardedHeaders`, or list the public origin in `AllowedActionOrigins`.

A page action that receives a form posted from another site (a payment or identity provider posting back) can turn both checks off with `.DisableAntiforgery()`. Check the post some other way, such as the provider's signature. On a server action `.DisableAntiforgery()` turns off the token check only; its origin check stays.

The antiforgery cookie keeps ASP.NET Core's defaults (`SameSite=Strict`, `HttpOnly`), so the same app works over plain HTTP in development. An app served only over HTTPS should make it a `__Host-` cookie, which a sibling subdomain or a plain-HTTP response cannot set or replace:

```csharp
builder.Services.AddAntiforgery(o =>
{
    o.Cookie.Name = "__Host-Antiforgery";
    o.Cookie.SecurePolicy = CookieSecurePolicy.Always;
    o.Cookie.Path = "/"; // __Host- cookies need it, also under UsePathBase
});
```

With `SecurePolicy.Always`, ASP.NET Core refuses every antiforgery operation on a request that is not HTTPS (a 500), so behind a TLS-terminating proxy call `UseForwardedHeaders` first, and keep the default in development.

### Body limits

A server action's request body may be at most 1 MB (`NetjesOptions.ActionBodySizeLimit`, like Next.js's `serverActions.bodySizeLimit`); a larger one gets 413. The option only lowers the server's own limit (Kestrel's is 30 MB). Page actions keep the server's limit. An action that takes uploads sets its own with `[RequestSizeLimit(bytes)]`. [Body limits](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/actions-and-forms.md#body-limits) has the details.

### What a failed post hands back

A form whose action fails validation comes back with what was typed, so the user does not type it again. Only the fields the action declares come back, never files, and never a field whose name contains one of the words in `NetjesOptions.PrivateFormFields` (`password`, `token`, `card`, `pin`, `iban` and more). What comes back goes out `Cache-Control: no-store`: the page rendered again, or a server action's answer to a call from the client. [What a failed post hands back](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/actions-and-forms.md#what-a-failed-post-hands-back) has the default words, how they match and the size limits.

The return page of a post without JavaScript is always a page of the app: a return URL that routes anywhere else renders the home page (or the error page with 422, where `/` is no page either). Middleware registered before `UseNetjes()` does not run again for that render, so protect pages with endpoint authorization, not with middleware ahead of `UseNetjes()` ([Forms without JavaScript](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/actions-and-forms.md#forms-without-javascript)).

## Redirects

`Page.Redirect(url)` and `ServerAction.Redirect(url)` accept relative URLs and absolute `http` and `https` URLs, and throw for anything else, including a `%` before the first `:` or `/`, which could hide an encoded scheme (`javascript%3A`). Start a relative URL with `/` or `./`.

For a URL that comes from the request, such as a `returnUrl` query value, use `Page.LocalRedirect(url)`: it throws unless the URL is a path on this site (`/path`, not `//host` or `/\host`). `Page.IsLocalUrl(url)` checks one first, so you can fall back instead:

```csharp
return Page.IsLocalUrl(returnUrl) ? Page.LocalRedirect(returnUrl) : Page.Redirect("/");
```

The client router never loads a page from another origin: a redirect or link to another site is a full page load, handed to the browser.

## The image endpoint

`/_netjes/image` serves only the widths and qualities you configure, reads local images from `public/` only and only as their files are spelled, fetches remote images only from the hosts in `Netjes:Images:RemoteHosts` (https on the default port, public addresses only, no redirects followed, no proxy, within a size cap and a timeout), serves only PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP and AVIF bytes (SVG only with `AllowSvg`, sandboxed), and bounds how many images it reads, fetches and processes at once. The [images guide](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/images.md) has every limit and setting.

With `Netjes.Images.SkiaSharp`, native codecs parse whatever a file in `public/` or an allow-listed host holds, even limited to PNG, JPEG and WebP. Keep SkiaSharp current: when a fix ships before `Netjes.Images.SkiaSharp` moves to it, reference the newer `SkiaSharp` and `SkiaSharp.NativeAssets.Linux.NoDependencies` packages from your project.

## The Node sidecar

The Node processes that render pages listen on `127.0.0.1` only, on a random port. Each gets a random token from .NET when it starts and refuses every request without it (403); a process does not start without one. The process removes the token from its environment before any page code runs. If you start `sidecar/server.mjs` yourself, set `NETJES_TOKEN` to a non-empty value and send it as the `X-Netjes-Token` header.

Page code that runs on the server runs in those processes, not in .NET. It sees the environment the app was started with, except the token.

## The layout key secret

On client navigations the router sends keys for the layouts it already shows, and the server skips the loaders of those layouts while the keys still match. A key is an HMAC of the layout's folder, the build, the user (authentication type, name, identifier and roles) and the layout's own route values, signed with `NetjesOptions.SegmentKeySecret`, so a client cannot make up a key for a layout it was not given, or reuse one across users.

- By default the secret is random per process. Set it, at least 32 bytes, when several instances should accept each other's keys (see [deployment](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/deployment.md#several-instances)); a shorter one stops the app at startup. Keep it out of source control like any secret.
- A layout loader binds only the route values of its own URL, and is skipped while they and the user stay the same. So an access check on a route value deeper than the layout's URL belongs in the page's loader, which runs on every navigation. [Data loading](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/data-loading.md) explains this.

## Hosts and HTTPS

- `AllowedHosts`: the template's `appsettings.json` allows any host (`*`), and its `appsettings.Development.json` allows only `localhost;127.0.0.1;[::1]`, so a page that rebinds its DNS name to your machine cannot reach the dev app. Pin `AllowedHosts` to your host names in production: the output cache keys entries on the host, and every made-up host would otherwise get entries of its own.
- HSTS and HTTPS redirection are ASP.NET Core's. The template calls `UseHsts()` and `UseHttpsRedirection()` outside Development.
- Behind a proxy that terminates TLS, call `UseForwardedHeaders()` first, trusting only that proxy's network, so the app sees the original scheme, host and client address. [Deployment](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/deployment.md#proxies-and-base-paths) has an example.

## Errors and configuration

- Error pages show exception messages and stacks only in Development (`IncludeErrorDetails`). In production an `error.tsx` gets the status's reason phrase as `error.message`.
- Everything in `Netjes:PublicConfig` is sent to the browser as it is. Never put a secret there.
- Output-cached pages are served to every visitor; keep per-visitor data out of them. See [caching](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/caching.md#shared-props-and-cookies).

## The development server

The Vite dev server binds to `localhost`. `NETJES_VITE_HOST=0.0.0.0` (in the environment of `npm run dev`) exposes it to the network, and with it the workspace. The Vite plugin denies the backend's files to the dev server, on top of Vite's own list (`.env` files, certificates, `.git`): settings files, C# sources and build output, dev certificates and keys, SQLite databases and Compose files, all listed in the [Vite plugin reference](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/reference/vite-plugin.md#the-dev-server). Everything else under the workspace root (or your own `server.fs.allow`) is readable by anyone who can reach the port, so only expose it on a network you trust. The template's development Compose file binds its ports to `127.0.0.1`.

<!-- Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/deployment.md -->

# Deployment

This guide is for app developers taking a Netjes app to production: what `dotnet publish` produces and what the server needs, the template's Docker and Compose setup, configuration, running several instances behind a load balancer, health checks, telemetry and logs, and running behind a proxy or under a base path. Security settings to review before you go live are in [security](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/security.md).

## Build and publish

A Netjes app is an ASP.NET Core app with a client build next to it. `dotnet publish` makes both:

```bash
dotnet publish -c Release -o bin/publish
```

The build leaves `bin/`, `obj/` and a `publish/` folder in the project out of the app's content, so `-o publish` works as well as `-o bin/publish`. A folder with another name is not left out: the Web SDK takes the JSON and config files under the project folder as content, so it would be copied into the next build's output. The template's `.gitignore` and `.dockerignore` list `publish/`.
